title: Two sons, the elder and the younger
claim: A father near death with two sons named in elder/younger order; the younger departs for a distant province/country; rivalry with the elder over the father's estate/kingdom; the condemned younger son is spared and restored through a parent's intercession.
lukeQuote: And not many days after the younger son gathered all together, and took his journey into a far country, and there wasted his substance with riotous living.
anabQuote: Darius and Parysatis had two sons: the elder was named Artaxerxes, and the younger Cyrus.
verification: Two sons, elder/younger named, the younger departing to a distant province — literal in both. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Typological framing: Cyrus as the prodigal who, instead of returning penitent to be received by the father, is received back 'in safety' by the mother and returns with an army.

title: A king with ten thousand against a greater king
claim: A man goes to war against a king; before battle he sits in council to consult; his force is ten thousand (10,400 Hellenes) against a vastly greater royal army (reported 1,200,000); Luke 14:32's 'ambassage' desiring terms matches the deputation the army sends to negotiate with Cyrus (Anab 1.3.19).
lukeQuote: Or what king, going to make war against another king, sitteth not down first, and consulteth whether he be able with ten thousand to meet him that cometh against him with twenty thousand?
anabQuote: Of Hellenes there were ten thousand four hundred heavy infantry with two thousand five hundred targeteers
verification: 10,400 Hellenes, a council of war before battle, and a deputation to treat — Luke's scenario point for point. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: The Ten Thousand is the famous designation of this very army; Cyrus 'summoned the generals... and held a council of war' before the battle (Anab 1.7.1).

title: The claimant travels for a kingdom; word is sent to the king against him
claim: A nobleman journeys toward a kingship (Cyrus marches up-country to make himself king in his brother's stead, Anab 1.1.1); those who will not have him reign send a message ahead to the king denouncing him; on victory the claimant's enemies are to be slain before him (Luke 19:27), as Orontas is condemned and led out before Cyrus (Anab 1.6).
lukeQuote: But his citizens hated him, and sent a message after him, saying, We will not have this man to reign over us.
anabQuote: An equipment so large pointed to something more than an invasion of Pisidia: so he argued; and with what speed he might, he set off to the king, attended by about five hundred horse.
verification: Structural correspondence assembled across sections; the message-to-the-king element is literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Parable of the pounds; note the same section of Xenophon calls loyalty to Cyrus 'a more profitable investment than so many pounds a month' (Anab 1.9.13, translation).

title: Soldiers demanding their wages
claim: Soldiers as a class come demanding concerning their pay; the issue is contentment with wages — Cyrus's soldiers, months in arrears, repeatedly demand their dues at the palace gates and are put off with fine words.
lukeQuote: And the soldiers likewise demanded of him, saying, And what shall we do? And he said unto them, Do violence to no man, neither accuse any falsely; and be content with your wages.
anabQuote: the soldiers, whose pay was now more than three months in arrear, came several times to the palace gates demanding their dues
verification: Soldiers as a class demanding their pay, contentment with wages at issue — literal in both. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Later the whole mutiny at Tarsus is settled by a raise of half a daric a month (Anab 1.3.21) — soldiers made content with their wages.

title: One hundred lost in the wild hills
claim: Exactly one hundred lost; separated from the main body in wild/mountain country; described as having gone astray; the question of whether anyone goes after that which is lost — here no one does and they perish.
lukeQuote: What man of you, having an hundred sheep, if he lose one of them, doth not leave the ninety and nine in the wilderness, and go after that which is lost, until he find it?
anabQuote: being unable to overtake the main body, or discover the route, had gone astray and perished. However it was, they numbered one hundred hoplites
verification: The number (one hundred gone astray) is literal, but the roles are inverted: the hundred are lost and none retrieved. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Typological inversion: the hundred that stray from Menon's flock are abandoned and perish, where Luke's shepherd retrieves the strayed from the hundred.

title: The maimed, the halt, and the blind on the highways
claim: Public highways populated by men lacking hand, foot, or eye — precisely Luke's 'maimed... halt... blind,' whom the servants are sent to gather 'into the highways' (Luke 14:23).
lukeQuote: Go out quickly into the streets and lanes of the city, and bring in hither the poor, and the maimed, and the halt, and the blind.
anabQuote: It was no rare sight to see on the well-trodden highways, men who had forfeited hand or foot or eye
verification: Men who forfeited hand, foot or eye on the well-trodden highways — Luke's maimed, halt and blind, literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Typological inversion: Cyrus's justice produces the amputees who line the highways; Luke's banquet-lord sends to the highways to gather them in.

title: The faithful steward made ruler over more
claim: A steward who furnishes his charge well and is found just/faithful; the lord's response is to enlarge his rule and possessions (Luke 12:44 'ruler over all that he hath'; cf. Luke 19:17 'authority over ten cities').
lukeQuote: Who then is that faithful and wise steward, whom his lord shall make ruler over his household, to give them their portion of meat in due season?
anabQuote: if he saw any skilful and just steward who furnished well the country over which he ruled, and created revenues
verification: A 'skilful and just steward' promoted to rule more — same role-word, same criterion. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Same role-word 'steward' in translation; both texts make faithful stewardship the criterion for promotion to greater rule.

title: To him who hath shall be given
claim: The identical maxim of reward: the lord, far from taking from the productive man, gives more to the one who already has.
lukeQuote: For I say unto you, That unto every one which hath shall be given; and from him that hath not, even that he hath shall be taken away from him.
anabQuote: so far from robbing him at any time, to him who had, he delighted to give more
verification: 'To him who had, he delighted to give more' — the maxim near-verbatim, in the same steward context. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Near-verbatim coincidence of the proverb in translation ('to him who had... give more' / 'unto every one which hath shall be given'), in the same context of a lord assessing stewards.

title: Whithersoever thou goest, I go also
claim: A pledge of unconditional following, spoken on the road at a crisis of allegiance: 'I will follow thee whithersoever thou goest' beside Clearchus's 'Wherever you go, I go also' — both preceding warnings about the hardship of the way.
lukeQuote: And it came to pass, that, as they went in the way, a certain man said unto him, Lord, I will follow thee whithersoever thou goest.
anabQuote: My decision is taken. Wherever you go, I go also.
verification: 'Wherever you go, I go also' — the pledge formula, literal in both. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Clearchus also says 'Whatever betide, I will share your fate. I look upon you as my country, my friends' — cf. leaving country and kin to follow (Luke 9:59-62).

title: All the kingdoms of the world offered for allegiance
claim: A leader displays the whole mapped-out extent of an empire and promises to give dominion over its territories to those who cast their lot with him in the coming contest; explicit gift of power and glory (the same speech promises 'to each of you Hellenes I will give a crown of gold').
lukeQuote: And the devil said unto him, All this power will I give thee, and the glory of them: for that is delivered unto me; and to whomsoever I will I give it.
anabQuote: all the intervening space is mapped out in satrapies belonging to my brother's friends: so that if the victory be ours, it will be ours also to put our friends in possession in their room
verification: Dominion offered for allegiance is literal; the panoramic-temptation frame is interpretive. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Typological framing: Cyrus as the tempter, surveying the world from its hot south to its frozen north and offering it in exchange for following him.

title: The table-companions who continue with him to the death
claim: The leader's inner circle is defined by his table ('table-companions'); they continue with him through his final trial and fall at his side; exactly one of the circle defects at the crisis (Ariaeus flees; Judas departs the table).
lukeQuote: That ye may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom, and sit on thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel.
anabQuote: fighting for his life beside him fell also every one of his faithful bodyguard of friends and table-companions, with the sole exception of Ariaeus
verification: The 'table-companions' fall at his side, sole exception the one who defects — literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Luke 22:28 'Ye are they which have continued with me in my temptations' immediately precedes the table promise; Xenophon's eulogy makes dying at the table-fellow's side the proof of the leader's worth.

title: The cup of wine given to friends with a saying
claim: A leader takes a single vessel of wine and gives it to his friends with a fixed spoken formula, directing that it be drunk that very day among companions; the same passage has him distributing half loaves of bread with the message 'he hopes you will taste it yourself' (cf. the bread 'given for you,' Luke 22:19).
lukeQuote: And he took the cup, and gave thanks, and said, Take this, and divide it among yourselves:
anabQuote: he would send the half remaining flagon to some friend with a message to say: "Cyrus says, this is the best wine he has tasted for a long time, that is his excuse for sending it to you.
verification: Wine and half-loaves sent to friends with a first-person saying; the institution framing is interpretive. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Both are institution-like scenes: wine plus bread, distributed by the lord to his friends, each accompanied by a reported first-person saying of the giver.

title: No body, no tomb
claim: A condemned man is led away to death while onlookers bow down before him (cf. the mock homage of Luke 23:11); afterward no one ever sees him alive or dead, no one can declare the manner of his death, and no tomb is ever seen — the mirror image of the missing body and empty sepulchre.
lukeQuote: And they entered in, and found not the body of the Lord Jesus.
anabQuote: No one, of his own knowledge, could declare the manner of his death; though some conjectured one thing and some another. No tomb to mark his resting-place, either then or since, was ever seen.
verification: Missing tomb and unknown manner of death (Orontas), inverted against the empty tomb. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Typological inversion of the resurrection narrative. Note also the bodily sign marking him for death — each companion 'took him by the girdle; which is as much as to say, Let him die the death' — beside Judas marking Jesus for arrest with a kiss (Luke 22:47-48).

title: Midnight watch for the coming king
claim: Servants/soldiers mustered and kept in readiness in the night watches because the king/lord is expected to arrive; the king in fact comes at an unlooked-for hour — before the breakfast halt (Anab 1.10.19), 'at an hour when ye think not' (Luke 12:40).
lukeQuote: And if he shall come in the second watch, or come in the third watch, and find them so, blessed are those servants.
anabQuote: about midnight, Cyrus held a review of the Hellenes and Asiatics in the plain, expecting that the king would arrive the following day with his army to offer battle
verification: Midnight muster expecting the king, who then arrives at an unlooked-for hour — literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Shared elements: midnight readiness review, an expected royal coming, and the actual arrival catching the army unprepared (Anab 1.8.1: 'The king is advancing... before they could form their lines').

title: The water submits to him
claim: A body of water miraculously yields to the leader before his followers: the Euphrates, never before fordable without boats, 'retired before the face of Cyrus' so none was wetted above the chest; witnesses call it a miracle and read it as a sign of who the man is (future king / 'What manner of man is this').
lukeQuote: What manner of man is this! for he commandeth even the winds and water, and they obey him.
anabQuote: Thus the passage was looked upon as a thing miraculous; the river had manifestly retired before the face of Cyrus, like a courtier bowing to his future king.
verification: The river 'retired before the face of Cyrus... miraculous... future king' — nature certifying kingship, in the text's own words. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Both scenes use nature's obedience to certify royal identity; Xenophon's own text supplies the word 'miraculous.'

title: The strait gate that cannot be forced
claim: A narrow gated entrance ('the gates of Cilicia and Syria') that those who seek to enter by strength shall not be able to force; passage is only obtained by being admitted, not by striving with force.
lukeQuote: Strive to enter in at the strait gate: for many, I say unto you, will seek to enter in, and shall not be able.
anabQuote: To force a passage here would be impossible, so narrow was the pass itself, with the fortification walls stretching down to the sea, and precipitous rocks above; while both fortresses were furnished with gates.
verification: Narrow gated pass, entry by force declared impossible — elements literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Shared image: narrowness plus a gate plus the explicit statement that entry will be sought and not obtained by force.

title: Requite my foes: the anti-beatitude prayer
claim: A formal prayer/maxim on the treatment of friends and enemies, point-for-point inverted: Cyrus prays to live long enough to recompense friends and requite foes with a strong arm; Luke commands love of enemies and prayer for abusers.
lukeQuote: But I say unto you which hear, Love your enemies, do good to them which hate you,
anabQuote: The prayer has been attributed to him, "God grant I may live along enough to recompense my friends and requite my foes with a strong arm."
verification: Programmatic friends/enemies maxim, point-for-point inverted. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Typological inversion: both are programmatic ethical sayings attributed to the hero, on the identical friends/enemies axis. ('along' is the source file's spelling.)

title: The sent leader stoned by his own people
claim: The one sent to lead the people forward is pelted with stones by the very people he tries to gather and lead; their refusal is the point — the soldiers 'would not' follow, as Jerusalem 'would not' be gathered.
lukeQuote: O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, which killest the prophets, and stonest them that are sent unto thee; how often would I have gathered thy children together, as a hen doth gather her brood under her wings, and ye would not!
anabQuote: they began to pelt him and his baggage train, and Clearchus had a narrow escape of being stoned to death there and then
verification: Clearchus nearly stoned to death by the very men he would lead — literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Cf. also Luke 4:28-29, the attempt to destroy Jesus when he presses an unwelcome course on his own people.

title: He stood and wept before those who refused him
claim: Immediately after the rejection, the leader publicly weeps before the assembled people who will not go his way, while they look on — grief staged before the refusers themselves.
lukeQuote: And when he was come near, he beheld the city, and wept over it,
anabQuote: for a long while he stood and wept, while the men gazed in silent astonishment
verification: 'For a long while he stood and wept' before the refusers — the weeping-over-Jerusalem tableau. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Same episode as the stoning entry (Anab 1.3.1): rejection, attempted stoning, then public weeping — the Luke sequence (13:34; 19:41) distributed across one Xenophon scene.

title: They knew not he was dead; seeking the living among the dead
claim: At the close of the fatal day the followers marvel that their lord is nowhere to be seen and no messenger has come; they hold a mistaken belief about whether he lives — the Greeks assume the dead Cyrus is alive, the women at the tomb are told the missing Jesus is alive.
lukeQuote: And when they found not his body, they came, saying, that they had also seen a vision of angels, which said that he was alive.
anabQuote: marvelling the while that Cyrus was not anywhere to be seen, and that no messenger had come from him. For they were in complete ignorance of his death
verification: Ignorance of the leader's death, inverted (the dead man thought alive). Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Typological inversion of Luke 24:5 'Why seek ye the living among the dead?' — the Hellenes seek the dead among the living.

title: The queen who comes to the great one with treasure
claim: A foreign queen journeys to visit the famed ruler; great wealth passes between them; she is shown his greatness in a staged display (the review of the army held for her amusement, Anab 1.2.14-18).
lukeQuote: The queen of the south shall rise up in the judgment with the men of this generation, and condemn them: for she came from the utmost parts of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon
anabQuote: At this point Epyaxa, the wife of Syennesis, the king of the Cilicians, arrived on a visit to Cyrus; and it was said that Cyrus received a large gift of money from the queen.
verification: Visiting queen and wealth exchanged; the Solomon typology is interpretive. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Solomon typology: visiting queen, exchange of riches, exhibition of the ruler's glory; Epyaxa comes from the south (Cilicia) relative to Cyrus's line of march.

title: Fish as gods; the risen God eats a fish
claim: Fish placed in a divine register: the Syrians' river fish are gods that must not be injured, while Luke's risen Lord proves his bodily reality by eating a fish; the same Anabasis sentence pairs the sacred fish with sacred pigeons, as Luke pairs Jesus with sacrificial pigeons at his presentation (Luke 2:24).
lukeQuote: And they gave him a piece of a broiled fish, and of an honeycomb.
anabQuote: stocked with tame fish which the Syrians regard as gods, and will not suffer to be injured--and so too the pigeons of the place
verification: Sacred fish that must not be injured, inverted against the risen one eating a fish. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Typological inversion in Atwill's manner (cf. his 'eat my flesh'/cannibalism pairing): where Syrians will not injure the divine fish, Luke's divine one consumes the fish; double cultic-animal match (fish + pigeons).

title: Crying 'I repent' — forgiven twice, killed the third time
claim: An offender against his lord who turns again crying out that he repents; the wronged lord formally receives him back with pledges — twice; the pattern of repeat trespass and repeated restoration, terminated at the third offense by execution ('now for the third time, you have been detected in a treasonous plot').
lukeQuote: And if he trespass against thee seven times in a day, and seven times in a day turn again to thee, saying, I repent; thou shalt forgive him.
anabQuote: did you flee to the altar of Artemis, crying out that you repented? and did you thus work upon my feelings, that we a second time shook hands and made interchange of solemn pledges?
verification: Repeat penitent restored twice then executed at the third offense — limit-case inversion. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Typological inversion: Luke commands unlimited forgiveness of the repeat penitent; Cyrus's court-martial of Orontas dramatizes its limit at the third trespass.

title: Where the body is, there the eagle
claim: Luke's disciples ask 'Where, Lord?' and are answered with an eagle gathered to the body; on the field where Cyrus's body lies among the slain, what marks the spot is the royal standard — a golden eagle with wings extended, raised aloft on a lance.
lukeQuote: And they answered and said unto him, Where, Lord? And he said unto them, Wheresoever the body is, thither will the eagles be gathered together.
anabQuote: the royal standard, a kind of golden eagle, with wings extended, perched on a bar of wood and raised upon a lance
verification: Golden-eagle standard over the corpse-strewn field — the juxtaposition is constructed. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: The eagle standard stands over the battlefield of corpses on the very day Cyrus's body lies headless nearby (Anab 1.10.1) — the eagle gathered where the body is.

title: With me in paradise: the royal park with a river through its midst
claim: Xenophon's 'park' renders Greek paradeisos — the very word Luke uses for 'paradise'; a royal paradise belonging to the king's son, with a river flowing through the midst of it and its springs within the palace (an Edenic image), where the prince himself goes about in it.
lukeQuote: And Jesus said unto him, Verily I say unto thee, To day shalt thou be with me in paradise.
anabQuote: a large park full of wild beasts, which he used to hunt on horseback, whenever he wished to give himself or his horses exercise. Through the midst of the park flows the river Maeander
verification: paradeisos wordplay (flagged): Luke's word for paradise is Xenophon's word for these parks. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: WORDPLAY FLAG: the link runs through the Greek word paradeisos behind the English 'park'; the promise 'with me in paradise' set beside the prince who keeps company in his paradeisos. Cyrus later cuts down another such park and burns its palace (Anab 1.4.10) — paradise destroyed.

title: Thine enemies shall cast a trench
claim: The identical military measure in the same idiom: an enemy king, hearing of the adversary's approach, casts a great trench as a line of defence to shut him out/in — Luke's siege prophecy uses the KJV phrase 'cast a trench about thee' with 'keep thee in on every side.'
lukeQuote: For the days shall come upon thee, that thine enemies shall cast a trench about thee, and compass thee round, and keep thee in on every side,
anabQuote: The trench itself had been constructed by the great king upon hearing of Cyrus's approach, to serve as a line of defence.
verification: A defensive trench cast by the enemy king upon hearing of the approach — same earthwork, same idiom. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: The trench (thirty feet broad, eighteen deep, running to the wall of Media, Anab 1.7.14) is dug by 'thine enemies' against the approaching one; in Luke the same earthwork is turned against Jerusalem.

title: The betrayal supper
claim: A leader is invited to a friendly meal by the very party plotting his destruction; the treachery is consummated at/immediately after the shared table. Tissaphernes dines Clearchus with 'kindliest expression' and then has him seized; Jesus announces at supper that the betrayer's hand is on the table.
lukeQuote: But, behold, the hand of him that betrayeth me is with me on the table.
anabQuote: Tissaphernes, with kindliest expression, invited Clearchus to remain with him at the time, and entertained him at dinner
verification: Dinner as the lure; the treachery consummated at and immediately after the shared table — literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Core betrayal-at-table typology; the dinner in Anabasis is the lure that leads directly to the arrest, as the supper in Luke precedes the arrest that same night.

title: Seizure at a prearranged sign under a token of friendship
claim: Leaders who came trusting pledges of friendship are seized at a single prearranged signal; in Luke the friendly token (a kiss from an intimate) is itself the sign by which the seizure is triggered; those around the seized leaders are struck down / an ear is cut off.
lukeQuote: behold a multitude, and he that was called Judas, one of the twelve, went before them, and drew near unto Jesus to kiss him.
anabQuote: at one and the same signal, those within were seized and those without cut down
verification: Seizure at one prearranged signal, under pledges of friendship — literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Both arrests occur under an active truce/bond of friendship (oaths and right hands in Anabasis; the kiss in Luke).

title: A covenant sealed in sacrificial blood, then broken by a covenant partner
claim: At a night meeting, two parties swear 'not to betray one another' and ratify the covenant in the blood of slain victims (sword dipped in blood / cup of blood 'shed for you'); in both stories a sworn partner of the blood covenant (Ariaeus; Judas at the cup) betrays it.
lukeQuote: This cup is the new testament in my blood, which is shed for you.
anabQuote: The oaths were ratified by the sacrifice of a bull, a wolf, a boar, and a ram over a shield. The Hellenes dipped a sword, the barbarians a lance, into the blood of the victims.
verification: A covenant 'not to betray' ratified in the victims' blood, then broken by a sworn partner — literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: The Anabasis oath is explicitly 'not to betray one another'; typologically the new covenant in blood replaces the failed animal-blood covenant.

title: Armed force by night from the park to take the leaders
claim: After supper, in the evening, a body of armed men lurks in a park/garden to fall upon the leaders at night; the danger is framed as belonging to the night ('attack you in the night' / 'your hour, and the power of darkness').
lukeQuote: When I was daily with you in the temple, ye stretched forth no hands against me: but this is your hour, and the power of darkness.
anabQuote: They warn you to be on your guard, in case the barbarians attack you in the night. There is a large body of troops in the neighbouring park.
verification: Troops lurking in the park at night; Luke's arrest has the night but the garden element is Anabasis-side only. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Mirrors the calibration example 'seized in a garden': troops hidden in a park at night as instrument against the leaders.

title: Two men walking after supper joined by a stranger with a revelation
claim: Two named companions (Proxenus and Xenophon / Cleopas and companion) walk after supper; an unknown man draws near seeking them and delivers a message about hidden treachery/deliverance; the sought one answers 'I am he, whom you seek' (in Luke, inverted: the approaching stranger is himself the sought master).
lukeQuote: while they communed together and reasoned, Jesus himself drew near, and went with them.
anabQuote: Proxenus and Xenophon were walking in front of the place d'armes, when a man came up and demanded of the advanced guard where he could find Proxenus or Clearchus
verification: Two walkers joined by a seeking stranger — the inversion does the work. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Typological inversion: in Anabasis the stranger seeks the two walkers; in Luke the 'stranger' is the one they seek. The Anabasis scene contains the recognition formula 'I am he, whom you seek.'

title: The innocent leader officially reckoned a transgressor and executed
claim: The executed leader is publicly branded a covenant-breaker/criminal to justify his death: Clearchus 'shown' a perjurer and truce-breaker (falsely, per the narrator), Jesus 'reckoned among the transgressors'; in both, the announcement is made to his stunned followers.
lukeQuote: this that is written must yet be accomplished in me, And he was reckoned among the transgressors
anabQuote: Clearchus being shown to have committed perjury and to have broken the truce, has suffered the penalty, and he is dead
verification: The innocent leader officially branded a transgressor to justify the execution — literal in both. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Both texts insist on the victim's innocence while recording the official verdict of transgression.

title: Followers watching the destruction from afar, uncomprehending
claim: The followers of the seized leader(s) stand at a distance (camp / afar off) watching the fatal events unfold, unable to understand or intervene.
lukeQuote: And all his acquaintance, and the women that followed him from Galilee, stood afar off, beholding these things.
anabQuote: The Hellenes, as they looked from the camp, viewed that strange horsemanship with surprise, and could not explain to themselves what it all meant
verification: Followers watching the destruction from afar, unable to comprehend — same tableau, literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Same tableau: the community as distant, passive spectators of their leaders' destruction.

title: Leaders of the movement beheaded by the sovereign
claim: Men seized by a ruler's order are conveyed up to the sovereign and decapitated; Luke's Herod states he has beheaded John, the movement's forerunner; in both, the beheading is followed by anxious questions about who now leads/threatens.
lukeQuote: And Herod said, John have I beheaded: but who is this, of whom I hear such things?
anabQuote: The generals who were thus seized were taken up to the king and there decapitated
verification: The movement's leaders beheaded by the sovereign, with the anxious who-is-this sequel — literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Beheading as the king's instrument against charismatic leaders; both narratives immediately pivot to the successor figure.

title: The one guilty man exempted while the others are put to death
claim: At a collective condemnation, the conspicuously guilty man (Menon, who shared and indeed instigated the conduct / Barabbas, guilty of sedition and murder) is alone exempted from the common fate, while the innocent are delivered to death.
lukeQuote: And he released unto them him that for sedition and murder was cast into prison, whom they had desired; but he delivered Jesus to their will.
anabQuote: he alone, although he had shared their conduct, was exempted from their fate
verification: The one conspicuously guilty man alone exempted while the innocent die — elements literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Exact role-inversion of desert: the transgressor spared, the blameless executed.

title: The felon's death inverted into the felon's paradise
claim: Among those executed together, one is singled out for a different end; Anabasis's spared man ultimately 'died the death of a felon' in prolonged disgrace, while Luke's confessed felon ('we receive the due reward of our deeds') dies beside the innocent one and is promised paradise the same day.
lukeQuote: And we indeed justly; for we receive the due reward of our deeds: but this man hath done nothing amiss.
anabQuote: he lived for a year in pain and disgrace and died the death of a felon
verification: The felon's-death contrast requires the inversion to connect. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Typological inversion: prolonged felon's death as ultimate punishment versus same-day felon's translation to paradise; both passages contrast the speedy death of the others with the singled-out man's fate.

title: Menon as the Judas type: the friend-ensnarer who sells his own
claim: An insider among the leadership, insatiable for money, treats friendship itself as the instrument of betrayal, holds secret meetings with the enemy power (Menon with Tissaphernes / Judas with the chief priests), and is complicit in delivering his fellow leaders to death.
lukeQuote: And he went his way, and communed with the chief priests and captains, how he might betray him unto them.
anabQuote: If he called a man his friend it might be looked upon as certain that he was bent on ensnaring him
verification: Menon as the Judas type — a character-type correspondence. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Character-type parallel: Xenophon's obituary of Menon (wealth-obsessed, false-swearing, robbing 'a friend in the midst of his security') reads as a portrait of Luke's Judas, down to the disgraceful death recorded of each tradition's traitor.

title: Rulers called 'benefactors' amid the betrayal scenes
claim: The distinctive honorific 'benefactors' (Greek euergetai) applied to leaders in an authority dispute: spoken by Jesus at the last supper about Gentile kings, and by Xenophon of the seized generals whom the betrayers themselves admit to be 'good friends and benefactors.'
lukeQuote: The kings of the Gentiles exercise lordship over them; and they that exercise authority upon them are called benefactors.
anabQuote: where are Proxenus and Menon, our generals and your good friends and benefactors, as you admit? Send them back to us
verification: Leaders called 'benefactors' (euergetai), inside both betrayal narratives — lexical match in context. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Wordplay/lexical flag: rests on the shared Greek honorific euergetes rendered 'benefactors' in both English texts; both occurrences sit inside the respective betrayal narratives.

title: Deliberating war against the great king with ten thousand
claim: The explicit deliberation whether a force can 'wage a war with the king' against overwhelming numbers, hinging on the figure ten thousand, with the stated alternative of seeking terms/saving oneself (Luke's king 'sendeth an ambassage, and desireth conditions of peace'; the Greeks proceed to truce negotiations).
lukeQuote: what king, going to make war against another king, sitteth not down first, and consulteth whether he be able with ten thousand to meet him that cometh against him with twenty thousand?
anabQuote: if you have one chance, one hope in ten thousand to wage a war with the king successfully, do not give up your arms
verification: Ten thousand weighing war against the great king, then treating for peace — literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Number parallel flagged: Xenophon's army is traditionally 'the Ten Thousand,' facing exactly Luke's scenario of a smaller force counting the cost of war against a greater king, then treating for peace via envoys.

title: Keep your arms or lose your lives
claim: A crisis teaching that followers must now be armed because surrendered weapons mean forfeited lives: the king demands the Hellenes give up their arms and they refuse ('robbed of our lives'); Jesus reverses his earlier unarmed commission and orders the sword bought even at the cost of one's garment.
lukeQuote: he that hath no sword, let him sell his garment, and buy one.
anabQuote: If we keep the former we imagine we can make use of the latter; but if we deliver up our arms we shall presently be robbed of our lives
verification: Arms-equal-survival is literal in the Anabasis; Luke's sword purchase corresponds interpretively. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Same equation of weapons with survival on the eve of confrontation with the ruling power; in both scenes the arms question is the hinge of the negotiation.

title: The throne offered but his subjects will not have him reign
claim: A man is proposed for the king's throne, and the decisive objection is that his own people/peers 'will not suffer him' to reign; Luke's nobleman's citizens send word 'We will not have this man to reign over us.'
lukeQuote: But his citizens hated him, and sent a message after him, saying, We will not have this man to reign over us.
anabQuote: better than himself who will not suffer him to sit upon the king's throne
verification: Subjects refusing the claimant's kingship, the message carried back — literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: The Greeks had formally offered to 'place him on the king's throne' (2.1.4); the refusal message is carried back by envoys in both texts.

title: He who went to the king, received the dead rival's kingdom, and slew
claim: After the royal claimant's death, a man goes to the great king, receives the dead rival's power and territory in addition to his own, returns, and slays those subject to him who opposed him — the arc of Luke's nobleman who receives a kingdom, returns, and has his enemies slain before him.
lukeQuote: A certain nobleman went into a far country to receive for himself a kingdom, and to return.
anabQuote: the power which belonged to Cyrus and his territory are yours now. You have them, and your own satrapy besides, safe and sound
verification: Tissaphernes as the pounds-parable nobleman — structural typology. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Typological framing: Tissaphernes as the parable's nobleman — journeys to the king, is granted Cyrus's domain plus his own satrapy, then returns and destroys the generals; flagged as a looser structural typology.

title: The king's trenches and walls to hem them in and destroy them
claim: Fear/prophecy that the hostile king is even now digging trenches and raising walls to enclose the people and make escape impossible, as prelude to their destruction ('the king would give a great deal to destroy us' / 'shall lay thee even with the ground').
lukeQuote: thine enemies shall cast a trench about thee, and compass thee round, and keep thee in on every side,
anabQuote: he is not at this moment digging away at trenches, or running up walls, to make our path impassable
verification: Trenches and encircling walls dug to make the path impassable — same vocabulary as the siege prophecy. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Same siege-engineering vocabulary (trench + encircling works) deployed as an image of impending annihilation by the great power.

title: Dashed hope in the slain claimant
claim: Immediately after the leader's death, his followers voice their broken hope in him as the one who was to take the kingdom/redeem them ('Would that Cyrus were yet alive' / 'we trusted that it had been he'), while insisting the cause was in fact victorious.
lukeQuote: But we trusted that it had been he which should have redeemed Israel
anabQuote: Would that Cyrus were yet alive! But since he is dead, take back this answer to Ariaeus, that we, at any rate, have conquered the king
verification: 'Would that Cyrus were yet alive' beside 'we trusted that it had been he' — dashed hope in the slain claimant. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Typological inversion available: Cyrus stays dead and the hope collapses; Luke's lament is answered by resurrection.

title: Anxious waiting resolved on the third day by news of salvation
claim: After the crisis, the mediator is absent a day while the community is 'troubled'; on the third day the news arrives that deliverance has been granted ('permitted to save' / 'he was alive'), overturning the gainsayers who argued against letting them go in peace.
lukeQuote: to day is the third day since these things were done.
anabQuote: he did not come back, and the Hellenes were troubled with anxieties, but on the third day he arrived with the news that he had obtained from the king the boon he asked; he was permitted to save the Hellenes
verification: Anxiety, delay, and on the third day the news that he is 'permitted to save' — literal, number included. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Third-day salvation-announcement pattern; number parallel plus shared sequence of anxiety, delay, third-day tidings.

title: The loosed ass and the challenge answered by proclamation
claim: An ass turned loose becomes the object of a public question about who loosed/let it and why; an authoritative pronouncement (the generals' heralded reward / 'the Lord hath need of him') settles the matter and calms the crowd; money is attached to the ass in both (a talent of silver reward; the owners' surrendered property).
lukeQuote: And as they were loosing the colt, the owners thereof said unto them, Why loose ye the colt?
anabQuote: Whoever will give any information as to who let an ass into the camp shall receive a talent of silver in reward
verification: Loosed ass, the who-loosed-it question, the settling proclamation — the parody framing carries it. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Flagged comedic/parody framing in Atwill's manner: the triumphal colt scene as a play on the camp-ass proclamation; both hinge on the question of who loosed the animal.

title: Night terror at a supposed apparition proven baseless
claim: A group is seized at night by sudden collective terror attributed to an unseen visitation; their leader then demonstrates concretely that the fear is groundless (proclamation revealing the mundane cause and the generals 'safe and sound' / showing hands and feet and eating), and calm returns.
lukeQuote: But they were terrified and affrighted, and supposed that they had seen a spirit.
anabQuote: a panic seized them, and there was a noise and clatter, hardly to be explained except by the visitation of some sudden terror
verification: Night panic ascribed to an unseen visitation, then concretely shown groundless — literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Both scenes end with the demonstration that the leaders are alive and well; in Luke the 'visitation' is real, inverting the Anabasis debunking.

title: The wounded emissary returns; the leaders are killed
claim: Emissaries sent under a standing agreement are violently abused by the party bound to them; a wounded survivor comes back bearing the news (Nicarchus with his belly wound telling all that had happened / the third servant wounded and cast out), and the affair culminates in the killing of the chosen leaders/heir.
lukeQuote: And again he sent a third: and they wounded him also, and cast him out.
anabQuote: Nicarchus the Arcadian came tearing along for bare life with a wound in the belly, and clutching his protruding entrails in his hands
verification: The wounded returning emissary — the escalation pattern is structural. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Escalation pattern shared: repeated missions, wounding, then the murder of the principals; the gruesome returning messenger is the pivot in both.

title: Fear your own lord more than the enemy who merely kills
claim: A recorded maxim that the follower/soldier must fear his own master more than the external foe, because the master's power extends beyond what the enemy can do to the body; both frame obedience and readiness against the foe as products of that greater fear.
lukeQuote: But I will forewarn you whom ye shall fear: Fear him, which after he hath killed hath power to cast into hell; yea, I say unto you, Fear him.
anabQuote: the soldier who is to mount guard and keep his hands off his friends, and be ready to dash without a moment's hesitation against the foe--must fear his commander more than the enemy
verification: Fear your own master more than the enemy who merely kills — the same comparative maxim. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Aphorism-level parallel: identical comparative structure (fear X more than the killing enemy); flagged as a sayings match rather than narrative.

title: Laughed him to scorn
claim: The identical idiom 'laughed him to scorn' aimed at a figure presumed finished (the dead girl's mourners scorn Jesus; the Greeks boast of having laughed the king to scorn), followed in each case by a reversal that confounds the scorn (the girl raised; the king's vengeance).
lukeQuote: And they laughed him to scorn, knowing that she was dead.
anabQuote: a handful of men like ourselves beat the king at his own gates, laughed him to scorn, and then came home again
verification: 'Laughed him to scorn' — flagged as a translation artifact. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Wordplay/translation flag: the verbatim English idiom is an artifact of the translations, in the same way Atwill leans on English/Whiston phrasing; retained because the phrase is distinctive and both contexts invert the scorn.

title: The uncrossable barrier fixed between the two parties
claim: In a speech about the other party's helplessness, an impassable water barrier is said to lie between them which they cannot cross at all in either direction without the other side's leave ('unless we transport you' / 'they which would pass from hence to you cannot'), within a discourse of threatened torment (fire and famine in Tissaphernes's speech; flame and torment in Luke).
lukeQuote: between us and you there is a great gulf fixed: so that they which would pass from hence to you cannot; neither can they pass to us, that would come from thence.
anabQuote: there are some which you will not be able to cross at all, unless we transport you to the other side
verification: An impassable barrier fixed between the parties — flagged weakest; topographic allegory. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Flagged as the weakest inclusion: topographic-allegory match of the kind Atwill regularly draws between Josephus's geography and gospel imagery.

title: Friends arriving at midnight from a journey with nothing to set before them
claim: Travelers on a journey come to a friend at midnight, and the crisis is the total lack of food to set before the arrivals: the Hellenes reach Ariaeus's camp 'about midnight' and the immediate council concern is that 'we have no provisions whatsoever' (2.2.10).
lukeQuote: For a friend of mine in his journey is come to me, and I have nothing to set before him?
anabQuote: about midnight reached their first stage, having come up with Ariaeus and his army
verification: Midnight arrival with nothing to set before them — a lighter composite. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Three shared concrete elements (midnight arrival, friendship bond, absence of provisions); flagged as a lighter, secondary-tier claim.

title: Seek to save your life and lose it
claim: Identical paradox-aphorism: those who seek to save their lives die/lose them, those who accept death preserve life (attain old age / preserve it), delivered as exhortation before a mortal trial.
lukeQuote: Whosoever shall seek to save his life shall lose it; and whosoever shall lose his life shall preserve it.
anabQuote: they, who in matters of war seek in all ways to save their lives, are just they who, as a rule, die dishonourably
verification: The save-your-life-and-lose-it paradox, in both texts, as exhortation before mortal trial. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Xenophon continues that those who strive to die nobly 'more frequently... attain to old age' - the full save/lose inversion. No wordplay needed; near-verbatim conceptual match.

title: Eyes that see not, ears that hear not
claim: Distinctive double formula: having eyes yet not seeing/perceiving, having ears yet not hearing/understanding, used to rebuke the spiritually or politically obtuse.
lukeQuote: that seeing they might not see, and hearing they might not understand
anabQuote: though you have eyes to see, you do not perceive
verification: Eyes that see not and ears that hear not — both halves present in the speech. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: The Anabasis sentence continues into the next section: 'though you have ears to hear, you do not recollect' (Anab 3.1.27), completing both halves of the Lukan pair.

title: The king who cannot face ten thousand sends an embassy for peace
claim: A king going to war who cannot meet the opposing force sends an embassage desiring conditions of peace; the Anabasis is the story of the Ten Thousand, whom the Great King, unable to face, plied with embassies begging a truce.
lukeQuote: Or else, while the other is yet a great way off, he sendeth an ambassage, and desireth conditions of peace.
anabQuote: he was so at his wit's end, sending us embassies and begging for a truce, and furnishing provisions the while
verification: The king, unable to face the Ten Thousand, sends embassies begging truce — literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Number link: Luke's hypothetical army is ten thousand; Xenophon's host is the proverbial Ten Thousand ('ten thousand Clearchuses', Anab 3.2.31). Luke's parable reads as a precis of the campaign.

title: Betrayal at the shared table
claim: A leader is destroyed by a betrayer who first shares table-fellowship with him; hospitality and a pledge (right hand / kiss) are the instrument of the arrest.
lukeQuote: But, behold, the hand of him that betrayeth me is with me on the table.
anabQuote: after entertaining Clearchus at his own board as a friend, he used his hospitality to delude and decoy his victims
verification: Hospitality used to decoy; the pledged right hand becomes the betraying hand — literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Same section: Tissaphernes 'gave us the pledge of his right hand, and then, with a lie upon his lips... arrested our generals' - the hand given in friendship becomes the hand of betrayal, as in Luke the betrayer's hand is on the table.

title: He drew near as a friend, then struck
claim: An agent of the enemy approaches the company in the guise of friendship, professing loyalty and goodwill, and at the moment of closest contact the attack begins.
lukeQuote: behold a multitude, and he that was called Judas, one of the twelve, went before them, and drew near unto Jesus to kiss him
anabQuote: He approached the Hellenes as if he were friendly; but when they had got fairly to close quarters, all of a sudden some of them, whether mounted or on foot, began shooting
verification: Approach 'as if friendly,' violence at close quarters — literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Mithridates opens with 'I have been faithful... I am your well-wisher' before the ambush - the false friend's protestation. Typological: the kiss at close quarters = the friendly approach that turns to violence.

title: The corrupted officer who goes off in the night
claim: The enemy corrupts one officer from within the leader's own company; the suborned insider defects to the enemy by night, occasioning a resolution of open war without truce.
lukeQuote: Then entered Satan into Judas surnamed Iscariot, being of the number of the twelve.
anabQuote: they were even successful with one officer--Nicarchus, an Arcadian, who went off in the night with about twenty men
verification: The enemy corrupts one officer, who defects by night and precipitates the open breach — literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Both defections are attributed to outside corruption entering an insider ('they used to come and corrupt the soldiers' / Satan entered Judas), and both trigger the final open breach; Judas likewise slips away by night to the enemy.

title: Handed over trusting a pact, then beaten, goaded and insulted before death
claim: Leaders delivered unarmed into foreign hands under a formal assurance are then beaten, goaded with pricks, insulted, and held for a delayed, degrading death.
lukeQuote: For he shall be delivered unto the Gentiles, and shall be mocked, and spitefully entreated, and spitted on
anabQuote: went, trusting to the truce, unarmed to a conference with them, what came of it? what is happening at this instant? Beaten, goaded with pricks, insulted, poor souls, they cannot even die
verification: Delivered trusting a pact; beaten, goaded, insulted; the death itself deferred — literal, in sequence. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Same triple sequence: delivered up, abused (beaten/goaded/insulted vs mocked/entreated/spitted), then killed; in both the death itself is deferred beyond the abuse.

title: The rival king nailed to a cross
claim: The reigning power crucifies the man who claimed the kingship: the Persian king nails the body parts of his own brother, the royal claimant, to a cross; Rome crucifies the claimant placarded as King of the Jews.
lukeQuote: And a superscription also was written over him in letters of Greek, and Latin, and Hebrew, THIS IS THE KING OF THE JEWS.
anabQuote: when his own brother, the son of the same parents, was dead, was not content with that, but severed head and hand from the body, and nailed them to a cross
verification: The king nails his brother, the royal claimant, to a cross — pretender-on-a-cross, literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Same section adds that those who marched to unking the king can expect 'the extreme of ignominy and torture' as a public deterrent - the stated Roman rationale for crucifixion. Typological: pretender to the throne ends on a cross.

title: The bystander compelled by force to carry the burden and march
claim: During an uphill march to the decisive place, a reluctant man is compelled under physical duress by the crowd to take up the burden (shield/cross) and carry it as the leader presses on ahead on foot.
lukeQuote: they laid hold upon one Simon, a Cyrenian, coming out of the country, and on him they laid the cross, that he might bear it after Jesus
anabQuote: They gave him blows, they pelted him, they showered him with abuse, till they compelled him to take back his shield and march on
verification: A bystander compelled by blows to carry the burden up behind the leader — with the Soteridas/Soter name flagged. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Wordplay flag: the compelled man is Soteridas ('son of Soter/the Saviour'), who carries the burden immediately behind the leader of the salvation-march, as Simon bears the cross 'after Jesus' (Iesous = Saviour). Xenophon also dismounts and shoulders the load himself, the leader-as-burden-bearer.

title: The sun blotted out at the fall
claim: At the decisive fall (of the city / of the condemned king), a divinely sent darkness hides the face of the sun, lasting 'until' the consummation (until the inhabitants were gone out / until the ninth hour).
lukeQuote: And it was about the sixth hour, and there was a darkness over all the earth until the ninth hour.
anabQuote: then a cloud hid the face of the sun and blotted out the light thereof, until the inhabitants were gone out of the city, and so it was taken
verification: A cloud 'hid the face of the sun and blotted out the light thereof, until' the city fell — literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: The Larissa notice is itself written in biblical diction ('blotted out the light thereof'); in both texts the darkness is the god's own act marking the moment the stronghold is given over.

title: The great city besieged, taken by divine visitation, left desolate
claim: A great walled city is besieged by a king who cannot take it by strength or length of days; the god himself sends the stroke (amazement/desolation) and the city is taken and left an empty ruin.
lukeQuote: For the days shall come upon thee, that thine enemies shall cast a trench about thee, and compass thee round, and keep thee in on every side
anabQuote: the king of the Pesians laid siege, but could not take it either by length of days or strength of hand. But Zeus sent amazement on the inhabitants thereof, and so it was taken
verification: The siege fails until the god sends the stroke; the city is taken and left desolate — literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Mespila's colossal walls are catalogued and now stand deserted, as Jerusalem's admired stones will not be left 'one stone upon another' (Luke 19:44, 21:6); in both, the capture is theologized as the god handing over the city.

title: Sleepless agony by night; rousing the sleepers before the enemy comes
claim: On the night before falling into enemy hands, amid despair so deep that food is refused, the protagonist alone cannot sleep, rises in the dark, and rouses his prostrate companions with a rebuke about sleeping in the hour of crisis.
lukeQuote: Why sleep ye? rise and pray, lest ye enter into temptation.
anabQuote: Sleep, sirs, I cannot, nor can you, I fancy, nor lie here longer, when I see in what straits we are
verification: Despair, food refused, the sleepless leader rousing his prostrate companions before the seizure — literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Anab 3.1.3: 'with hearts full of despair, but few of them tasted food that evening... They could not close their eyes for very pain' - the Gethsemane tableau (agony, sorrow-sleep, imminent seizure by the enemy at night) point for point, inverted between leader and followers.

title: The council assembled at first light
claim: The all-night crisis (arrest of the leaders, night meetings) culminates in a formal plenary council convened at the first glimmer of day to determine the fate of the community/prisoner.
lukeQuote: And as soon as it was day, the elders of the people and the chief priests and the scribes came together, and led him into their council
anabQuote: the first faint glimmer of dawn had hardly commenced, as they met in the centre of the camp
verification: A formal council at first light following the night crisis — literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Sequence parallel with the preceding entry: seizure of leaders -> night gathering near midnight (Anab 3.1.33 'It was nearly midnight') -> dawn council. Typological inversion: one dawn council organizes salvation, the other condemnation.

title: The eighteen who fell
claim: Exactly eighteen men are singled out as overtaken by sudden calamity at a low place - eighteen crushed when the tower fell at Siloam, eighteen horsemen taken when driven down into the ravine.
lukeQuote: Or those eighteen, upon whom the tower in Siloam fell, and slew them, think ye that they were sinners above all men that dwelt in Jerusalem?
anabQuote: of their cavalry as many as eighteen were taken prisoners in the ravine
verification: Exactly eighteen fallen at a named low place — the number literal in both. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Number coincidence flagged as such; both eighteens are incidental casualty tallies attached to a named locale, and Luke returns to the number with the woman bound eighteen years (13:11).

title: The herds destroyed in the water
claim: Beside a body of water, a sudden enemy incursion onto the plain; men scattered abroad are cut down, and many herds of livestock are caught/perish in the water while crossing to the other side.
lukeQuote: and the herd ran violently down a steep place into the lake, and were choked
anabQuote: many herds of cattle had been caught whilst being conveyed across to the other side of the river
verification: Herds lost in the water during a sudden military irruption — the calibration claim-type, literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Calibration-type claim (Gadarene herd = animals lost in water during a military irruption). Same scene-elements: plain by the water, hostile force appearing suddenly, herds lost mid-crossing, dwellers' goods destroyed.

title: Wine-skins that must not burst: skins as salvation on the deep
claim: Wine-skins as the vessel on which everything depends: Luke's skins burst and perish if misused, the Rhodian's two thousand flayed and inflated skins, rightly used, are 'preserved' and keep every man from sinking in a river too deep to sound.
lukeQuote: And no man putteth new wine into old bottles; else the new wine will burst the bottles, and be spilled, and the bottles shall perish.
anabQuote: Two thousand wine-skins. I see there are plenty of sheep and goats and asses. They have only to be flayed, and their skins inflated
verification: Skins that perish against skins that save from perishing — the inversion carries it. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Typological inversion: skins that perish vs skins that save from perishing ('no danger of your drowning, for every skin will be able to support a couple of men without sinking'). The river is 'of such depth that they failed to reach the bottom' - cf. Luke's 'the deep' (5:4, 8:31).

title: Share with him that hath none; burn the rest
claim: A double command enacted: divest of superfluous goods, redistribute to each what he needs (he that hath two, impart to him that hath none), and commit the remainder to the fire.
lukeQuote: He that hath two coats, let him impart to him that hath none; and he that hath meat, let him do likewise.
anabQuote: after sharing with one another what each needed out of their various superfluities, they threw the remnant into the fire
verification: Share the surplus with him that hath none, burn the remnant — enacted in the one text, preached in the other. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: John's same sermon supplies the fire half of the pair ('the chaff he will burn with fire unquenchable', 3:17); the Anabasis narrates literally what the Baptist preaches: share out the surplus, burn the residue, travel light for the way.

title: Now buy weapons: the armed-poverty reversal
claim: At the moment peace/truce ends and open conflict begins, the leader reverses the company's prior unarmed economy and orders weapons to be obtained by purchase, paying money for arms; a small armed corps is then mustered.
lukeQuote: But now, he that hath a purse, let him take it, and likewise his scrip: and he that hath no sword, let him sell his garment, and buy one
anabQuote: who among them possess slings, and for these slings offer the owner the money value
verification: The truce over: weapons bought for money, a small corps mustered that night — literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Both scenes turn on the same hinge - 'but now' the truce is over, so equip yourselves - and both end with a token muster (Luke: 'here are two swords... It is enough'; Anab: 'that night two hundred slingers were enrolled').

title: Surveying the kingdom's wealth and glory as temptation
claim: A panoramic survey of the king's/kingdoms' territory, provisions, dependants, gold and apparel presented as a lure to the man of God/Hellas, who is restrained from taking it by a binding oath of allegiance.
lukeQuote: shewed unto him all the kingdoms of the world in a moment of time
anabQuote: I surveyed the extent and quality of their territory, the plenteousness of their provisions, the multitude of their dependants, their cattle, their gold, and their apparel
verification: Panoramic wealth surveyed as temptation, restrained by an oath — interpretive. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Typological framing: Xenophon 'pitied ourselves' amid the display 'yet our oath held us down' - as Jesus, shown the glory 'delivered unto me', holds to 'him only shalt thou serve'; in both, the goods are later promised as prizes only through the ordeal.

title: Luxury in a far country makes men forget the road home to the father(land)
claim: Men sojourning in a rich foreign land are warned that idleness, luxury and dalliance with its women will make them forget the road home; the remedy proposed is the resolve to return to their fathers'/native hearths.
lukeQuote: took his journey into a far country, and there wasted his substance with riotous living
anabQuote: if once we learn to live in idleness and to batten in luxury and dalliance with these tall and handsome Median and Persian women and maidens, we shall be like the Lotus-eaters, and forget the road home altogether
verification: Far-country luxury and the forgotten road home — prodigal typology. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Typological: the prodigal's arc (far country, dalliance with harlots, then 'I will arise and go to my father') tracks Xenophon's warning and the army's stated purpose 'to return to Hellas and to revisit our hearths and homes'.

title: Arrayed in finest apparel to face death, among men of war
claim: A man expecting death is clothed in his most splendid garments in an explicitly martial setting ('arrayed for war' / 'men of war'), the finery framed as fitting either victory or a noble end.
lukeQuote: And Herod with his men of war set him at nought, and mocked him, and arrayed him in a gorgeous robe
anabQuote: After him Xenophon arose; he was arrayed for war in his bravest apparel
verification: The doomed man in splendid apparel among men of war — the honor/mockery inversion does the work. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Typological inversion: Xenophon dresses himself in his best 'if I must needs die'; Herod's soldiers dress the condemned in gorgeous apparel as mockery - the same tableau of doomed man in splendid robes among warriors, honor inverted to derision.

title: A sign from heaven at the word of salvation, and worship of the Saviour
claim: At the very moment salvation is being proclaimed, a sudden sign from heaven appears; the whole assembly with one impulse bows in worship, and vows/praise are directed to the god under the title Saviour, with thank-offerings for deliverance.
lukeQuote: For unto you is born this day in the city of David a Saviour, which is Christ the Lord.
anabQuote: even as we spoke of safety, an omen from Zeus the Saviour has appeared, we vow a vow to sacrifice to the Saviour thank-offerings for safe deliverance
verification: A sign from heaven at the word of salvation; all bow; the Saviour title; thank-offerings vowed — literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Title flag: 'Zeus the Saviour' (Zeus Soter) / 'a Saviour (Soter)... the Lord'. In both, the sign triggers collective worship (soldiers 'with one impulse bowed in worship' and chanted the hymn / the heavenly host suddenly praising God).

title: The servant marked at the ears in the night crisis
claim: During the night crisis following the leaders' arrest, a hot-headed companion's intervention turns on a man's ear(s): the ears bored like a slave's expose him and he is cast out; the servant's ear is cut off by a disciple's sword.
lukeQuote: And one of them smote the servant of the high priest, and cut off his right ear.
anabQuote: this fellow has no connection either with Boeotia or with Hellas, none whatever. I have noted both his ears bored like a Lydian's
verification: Ears bored like a slave's beside the servant's severed ear — wordplay-adjacent. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Wordplay/culture flag: bored ears are the mark of a slave - the man exposed by his ears is servile, as the man wounded in the ear is a servant (doulos). Typological inversion: Agasias's ear-evidence expels the false brother; Jesus heals the struck ear and rebukes the sword.

title: One man become a military multitude: ten thousand Clearchuses / Legion
claim: A single person is identified with an army-sized multitude under one commander's name: the enemy will behold ten thousand Clearchuses instead of one; the possessed man answers to the name of a whole army unit, Legion, because many entered one.
lukeQuote: And he said, Legion: because many devils were entered into him.
anabQuote: on this day they will behold ten thousand Clearchuses instead of one
verification: Ten thousand Clearchuses against Legion — name-decode inversion, flagged. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Typological inversion flagged: one multiplied into a disciplined host to terrify the enemy vs a host compressed into one man to be expelled; in both the military mass-noun functions as a personal name and is aimed at striking fear.

title: Three days of cures on the journey
claim: In mid-journey under threat from a hostile ruler, the march halts for exactly three days devoted to healing (surgeons appointed for the wounded / I do cures), after which the protagonist must continue walking his route.
lukeQuote: Behold, I cast out devils, and I do cures to day and to morrow, and the third day I shall be perfected.
anabQuote: appointed eight surgeons to attend to the many wounded. Here they halted three days for the sake of the wounded
verification: The march halted exactly three days for the wounded, surgeons appointed, under a hostile ruler's pressure — literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Luke continues 'I must walk to day, and to morrow, and the day following' (13:33) - healing for a fixed three-day span embedded in a forced itinerary, with the hostile king (Herod/Tissaphernes) hanging on the traveller's skirts.

title: Honeycomb eaten by one risen from apparent death on the third day
claim: Honeycomb; men who ate the combs drop down 'apparently at death's door' and lie 'as if there had been a great defeat', then recover and stand on the third or fourth day; the risen Jesus, on the third day, proves he is not dead by eating a honeycomb before witnesses.
lukeQuote: And they gave him a piece of a broiled fish, and of an honeycomb.
anabQuote: But the next day, none had died; and almost at the same hour of the day at which they had eaten they recovered their senses, and on the third or fourth day got on their legs again
verification: Honey-eaters lie as if dead and stand again on the third or fourth day; the third-day risen one eats honeycomb — literal, inversion flagged. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Typological inversion: honey-eaters seem dead and rise the third day; the third-day risen one eats honey to show he lives. Same section says eaters 'dropped down, apparently at death's door.'

title: Two captives under death: the defiant one dies, the other confesses and opens the good road
claim: Exactly two prisoners facing death; interrogated; the first stays defiant and is killed before the eyes of his fellow; the second then speaks and promises 'I can take you by a good road' - as the second malefactor confesses and is promised entry to paradise while the railing one is condemned.
lukeQuote: And one of the malefactors which were hanged railed on him, saying, If thou be Christ, save thyself and us.
anabQuote: in spite of all sorts of terrors applied to extract a better answer--"no," he persisted. When nothing could be got out of him, he was killed before the eyes of his fellow
verification: Two captives; the defiant one killed before his fellow's eyes; the other then opens 'a good road' — literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Mirrors the calibration type 'three crucified with one surviving.' The surviving captive's 'good road, practicable even for beasts' is read typologically as the way/paradise granted to the cooperative one.

title: Terror-stricken horde plunges down into the deep and perishes
claim: A tormenting horde is seized with terror and hurls itself down into a depth (dell / lake) where all are extinguished ('not one of them ever uttered a sound again' / 'choked'); in both scenes this delivers tormented sufferers (the snow-blind invalids / the demoniac).
lukeQuote: the herd ran violently down a steep place into the lake, and were choked.
anabQuote: the enemy in terror hurled themselves through the snow into the dell, and not one of them ever uttered a sound again
verification: The terror-driven horde hurls itself into the depth and never utters a sound again — literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Direct analogue of the calibration example (Legion's swine drowning paired with drowning soldiers). Luke's demons beg 'not to go out into the deep'; Xenophon's enemies go into the dell and are silenced.

title: Cast down headlong from the height of one's own town
claim: The same rare action at the same setting: people of a hill-stronghold and a man are carried 'headlong' down from the brow/crags of the town's own height to death; Jesus escapes the identical fate attempted at Nazareth.
lukeQuote: led him unto the brow of the hill whereon their city was built, that they might cast him down headlong.
anabQuote: both were gone in an instant headlong down the crags, and were killed
verification: 'Headlong down the crags' at a hill stronghold — the Nazareth attempt, same action, same setting. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Inversion: at the Taochian fortress the rescuer (Aeneas) is dragged down and killed; at Nazareth the intended victim passes through the midst unharmed.

title: Mothers and infants perish at the fall of the stronghold; death sought from the heights
claim: At the capture of a doomed stronghold, women destroy their infants and themselves by throwing them from the height, the men likewise - enacting Luke's woe over daughters and sucklings at Jerusalem's fall and the plea 'to the mountains, Fall on us; and to the hills, Cover us.'
lukeQuote: Blessed are the barren, and the wombs that never bare, and the paps which never gave suck.
anabQuote: and then they cast themselves after their fallen little ones, and the men likewise
verification: The Taochian women casting their infants and themselves from the height — joined to Luke's woe typologically. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Typology: Luke's prophecy to the 'Daughters of Jerusalem' read as fulfilled in the Taochian women who cast their infants down the cliff and then leap after them.

title: Bound in fetters, and the bonds break of themselves
claim: A man bound in fetters whose bonds break/fall off without human agency, freeing his limbs; in both, the loosing immediately precedes a crossing of water to the far side (Xenophon's dream before the Centrites ford; the demoniac met after crossing the lake).
lukeQuote: he was kept bound with chains and in fetters; and he brake the bands, and was driven of the devil into the wilderness
anabQuote: In his sleep he thought that he was bound in fetters, but these, of their own accord, fell from off him, so that he was loosed, and could stretch his legs as freely as he wished.
verification: Fetters falling off of their own accord — in a dream, set against Luke's bodily demoniac. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Secondary echo: Luke 13:16, the woman 'whom Satan hath bound' who must 'be loosed from this bond.'

title: Sunk in perplexity, then at first light two young men announce the way is open
claim: A night halted 'sunk in perplexity' / women 'much perplexed'; at first light two young men suddenly appear and announce that the impossible passage is open; the news is met with ritual response (libations and prayer / bowing and worship) and reported to the leaders, who verify it.
lukeQuote: as they were much perplexed thereabout, behold, two men stood by them in shining garments
anabQuote: while Xenophon was taking his, two young men came running up to him
verification: Perplexity, then at first light two young men announce the impassable way open; worship follows — literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Resurrection-as-crossing typology: the two young men had stripped and crossed the 'impassable' river and returned to tell it, as the two men at the tomb declare the dead one risen and the way through death open.

title: A life-staked promise that within days they will see the goal from a mountain
claim: A solemn pledge staking life ('take my life' / 'not taste of death') that within a stated few days those present will see the longed-for goal; days later they ascend a mountain, see it, weep for joy, and build with stones on the summit (a great cairn / proposed three tabernacles).
lukeQuote: there be some standing here, which shall not taste of death, till they see the kingdom of God.
anabQuote: This guide told them that within five days he would lead them to a place from which they would see the sea, "and," he added, "if I fail of my word, you are free to take my life."
verification: A life-staked promise that within days they will see it; the mountain vision; stones raised on the summit — literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Transfiguration typology: 'The sea! the sea!' from Mount Theches as the vision of the kingdom; the cairn heaped and dedicated on the summit paired with Peter's offer to build three tabernacles.

title: Seventy sent forward in small groups ahead of the leader
claim: The exact number seventy, dispatched in advance of the leader into hostile ground, deliberately dispersed in small units (two and two / one by one) rather than as a body, preparing the way the leader himself is about to take.
lukeQuote: the Lord appointed other seventy also, and sent them two and two before his face into every city and place, whither he himself would come.
anabQuote: the next step was for a party of about seventy men to get away under the trees, not in a body, but one by one, every one using his best precaution
verification: Exactly seventy sent forward in small parties ahead of the leader — number and role literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Number coincidence plus shared role (advance party under fire, 'lambs among wolves' / men under a pelt of stones).

title: Fainting multitude in a desolate place fed by the leader's own hands and revived
claim: A hungry multitude collapsing in a desert/desolate march; the leader requisitions what food there is, distributes it with his own hands and through appointed agents (as Jesus gives to the disciples to set before the crowd), and the eaters immediately revive and go on.
lukeQuote: Send the multitude away, that they may go into the towns and country round about, and lodge, and get victuals: for we are here in a desert place.
anabQuote: laying an embargo on any eatables he could see, doled out with his own hands, or sent off other able-bodied agents to distribute to the sufferers, who as soon as they had taken a mouthful got on their legs again
verification: The fainting multitude in a desert place fed by the leader's own hands through appointed agents, instantly revived — literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Xenophon's men suffer 'boulimia (or hunger-faintness)'; the feeding scene is set, like Luke's, where the crowd cannot reach towns for victuals.

title: Eating human bodies at the threshold of the final trial
claim: Language of consuming human flesh spoken by the leader to his followers immediately before the last obstacle: Xenophon promises to 'swallow them up whole, without cooking'; Jesus at the last supper gives his body to be eaten before his passion.
lukeQuote: This is my body which is given for you: this do in remembrance of me.
