anabQuote: these men whom you see in front of you are the sole obstacles still interposed between us and the haven of our hopes so long deferred. We will swallow them up whole, without cooking, if we can.
verification: 'We will swallow them up whole' against the given body — inversion, flagged. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Same claim type as the calibration 'eat my flesh / cannibalism episode' pairing. Inversion flagged: eating enemies versus giving one's own body.

title: At the river: trees hewn down and a way prepared for the coming host
claim: At a river-crossing, trees are hewn down and a road is constructed to bring the people through; hostile parties are reconciled by exchanged pledges; the goal of the prepared way is 'to reach the sea' as Luke's prepared way ends 'all flesh shall see the salvation of God.'
lukeQuote: The voice of one crying in the wilderness, Prepare ye the way of the Lord, make his paths straight.
anabQuote: the Macrones fell to vigorously hewing down trees and constructing a road to help them across, mingling freely with the Hellenes
verification: Trees hewn down and a way constructed at the river — composite with the Baptist's sermon. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Luke 3:9's 'axe laid unto the root of the trees... hewn down' beside the Hellenes and Macrones felling the riverside trees; John's river-repentance scene paired with the riverside pledge-exchange.

title: The strong man's dwelling overcome and his spoils divided
claim: An armed magnate's residence is rushed and overcome; he flees and his trusted goods are taken as spoil - tent, silver-footed couches, goblets, horses, even his butlers and bakers - as in the parable the stronger one takes the armour 'wherein he trusted, and divideth his spoils.'
lukeQuote: when a stronger than he shall come upon him, and overcome him, he taketh from him all his armour wherein he trusted, and divideth his spoils.
anabQuote: as many as twenty horses were captured, with the tent of Tiribazus, and its contents, silver-footed couches and goblets, besides certain persons styling themselves the butlers and bakers
verification: The magnate's residence overcome, the trusted goods taken and divided as spoil — literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Parable-to-event pairing of the kind Atwill favors; Tiribazus 'the king's friend' keeping his palace-camp in peace until the stronger force comes upon him.

title: The king's intimate friend covenants peace, then plots a night seizure at the mount
claim: A figure defined by unique intimacy with the king (Tiribazus alone mounts the king on his horse / Judas, one of the twelve at the table) makes a formal covenant, then secretly organizes an armed force to fall upon the protagonists at a mount/defile; the plot is disclosed beforehand to the leaders.
lukeQuote: he went his way, and communed with the chief priests and captains, how he might betray him unto them.
anabQuote: Tiribazus had got it together," he added, "meaning to attack the Hellenes on the high mountain pass, in a defile which was the sole passage."
verification: The king's intimate covenants peace, then plots the night seizure at the pass — composite. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Inversion: forewarned, the Hellenes move by night and escape the pass; forewarned, Jesus goes by night to the mount and is taken. Tiribazus's treaty (Anab 4.4.5) supplies the covenant element.

title: The deserted leader's burden borne by another man
claim: Under a rain of blows/missiles the leader's own designated bearer abandons him and his burden; a bystander steps in, takes up the shield/cross, and bears it so the two go on together.
lukeQuote: they laid hold upon one Simon, a Cyrenian, coming out of the country, and on him they laid the cross, that he might bear it after Jesus.
anabQuote: Xenophon was left by his shield-bearer, who carried off his shield, but Eurylochus of Lusia, an Arcadian hoplite, ran up to him, and threw his shield in front to protect both of them
verification: Deserted by his own shield-bearer, another runs up and bears it for both — the Simon-of-Cyrene role, literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Role-parallel: the failed bearer (shield-bearer / the absent disciples) replaced by an outsider who carries the instrument for the protagonist during his descent under attack.

title: The falling stone that grinds a man to pieces
claim: A stone mass falling from above onto a man crushes him to pieces, literalizing 'on whomsoever it shall fall, it will grind him to powder'; both stones come from the rejected height (the crest abandoned and re-taken / the stone the builders rejected made the head).
lukeQuote: Whosoever shall fall upon that stone shall be broken; but on whomsoever it shall fall, it will grind him to powder.
anabQuote: They reached the summit of the mamelon from which Xenophon was descending, and began rolling down crags. One man's leg was crushed to pieces.
verification: The rolled crag that crushes a man 'to pieces' — the grinding stone, proverb-to-event. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Proverb-to-event pairing; cf. also Anab 4.7.1's men 'with their legs or ribs crushed to bits' by rolled stones.

title: In the night of extremity the leader finds his followers asleep with no watch
claim: During a night that decides survival, the leader comes upon his exhausted followers lying asleep, wrapped in their cloaks/for sorrow, with no watch kept; he rouses them and forces them up lest they perish in the trial.
lukeQuote: And when he rose up from prayer, and was come to his disciples, he found them sleeping for sorrow
anabQuote: they fell in with some soldiers who had laid down to rest on the snow with their cloaks wrapped round them
verification: In the night of extremity the followers lie asleep in their cloaks with no watch set, and are roused — literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: The Anabasis adds 'but never a guard was established' - the failed watch that Luke's 'rise and pray, lest ye enter into temptation' rebukes.

title: Compassed round and kept in on every side
claim: The people, quartered among dwellings, are encircled by enemies who ring them in and keep them under watch on every side through the night - the watch-fires 'in a circle... all round' enacting 'compass thee round, and keep thee in on every side.'
lukeQuote: thine enemies shall cast a trench about thee, and compass thee round, and keep thee in on every side
anabQuote: the Carduchians kept many watch-fires blazing in a circle on the mountains, and kept each other in sight all round
verification: Watch-fires blazing 'in a circle' all round — generic encirclement. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Luke's siege prophecy paired with a literal night encirclement, the same move Atwill makes with Josephus's siege lines.

title: At the army's approach, flee to the mountains with wives and children
claim: When the invading army appears, the inhabitants abandon their dwellings and flee to the mountains with their wives and children, leaving the houses and provisions behind - the precise instruction of Luke's apocalypse ('let them which are in Judaea flee to the mountains... depart out').
lukeQuote: Then let them which are in Judaea flee to the mountains; and let them which are in the midst of it depart out
anabQuote: the Carduchians abandoned their dwelling places, and with their wives and children fled to the mountains
verification: At the army's approach they abandon their dwellings and flee to the mountains with wives and children — literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Prophecy-to-enactment typology; the same section also supplies the abandoned 'stuff in the house' motif (goods left for the taking, Luke 17:31).

title: Petitioning the hostile power for the dead bodies, granted for honorable burial
claim: A formal approach to the enemy authority to beg back the dead body/bodies; the request is granted on terms; the dead are then given careful, customary honors ('they did everything for the dead... with the customary honours paid to good men' / wrapped in linen and laid in a new tomb).
lukeQuote: This man went unto Pilate, and begged the body of Jesus.
anabQuote: Xenophon held a colloquy with them by means of an interpreter, to negotiate a truce, and demanded back the dead bodies. These they agreed to restore
verification: A truce negotiated to demand back the dead bodies; granted; customary honors paid — literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Shared sequence: intercessor - hostile power - release of the body - burial rites; in both the request costs a concession (not burning the houses / Joseph's dissent from the council).

title: Left half dead by the wayside; the one who stops promises that care will come
claim: Travelers struck down and left by the wayside as the column passes on; the compassionate one turns aside, protects them from those who would finish them, and departs promising that others will come on the morrow to take care of them - which happens (Cheirisophus's men carry the sick into camp).
lukeQuote: Take care of him; and whatsoever thou spendest more, when I come again, I will repay thee.
anabQuote: Xenophon and his party, telling the sick folk that next day people would come for them, set off
verification: The sick left by the wayside; the one who stops promises that care will come on the morrow — and it does — literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Good Samaritan typology: the disabled 'were left to their fate' by those ahead (the priest/Levite role) before the rearguard leader stops and provides for morrow-care.

title: Latecomers at night refused fire and food unless they give in exchange
claim: Cold, late arrivals in the night beg those already settled for warmth and food; the settled refuse to give ('I cannot rise and give thee' / 'were not for allowing these late-comers near the fires'), and provision passes only through importunity or exchange of victuals.
lukeQuote: Trouble me not: the door is now shut, and my children are with me in bed; I cannot rise and give thee.
anabQuote: those who had arrived a good while and had kindled fires were not for allowing these late-comers near the fires, unless they would in return give a share of their corn or of any other victuals they might have
verification: Night latecomers refused fire and food unless they give in exchange — the midnight-loaves standoff, literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Parable-to-event pairing; the Anabasis continues 'Here then a general exchange of goods was set up,' the grudging giving that the parable's importunity finally extracts.

title: Questioned by serving women at night, they conceal who they are
claim: At night, arriving strangers are challenged by serving women (a maid by the fire / women and girls at the fountain) with the question of identity; a false answer is given ('I know him not' / 'They were on their way from the king to the satrap'), after which they pass inside the enclosure among the household.
lukeQuote: But a certain maid beheld him as he sat by the fire, and earnestly looked upon him, and said, This man was also with him.
anabQuote: surprised some women and girls who had come from the village to fetch water at the fountain outside the stockade. These asked them who they were. The interpreters answered for them in Persian
verification: The night identity-challenge by serving women, answered untruthfully — flagged weakest class. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Weakest class kept: shares night setting, female questioners, identity challenge, and untrue answer; flagged as an inversion (self-protective cover story rather than denial of a master).

title: Entering the dwelling from above through the opening in its roof
claim: Houses entered from above through an aperture in the top ('like the mouth of a well' / 'through the tiling'), the person descending into a broad interior 'in the midst' below; in both, beasts have their own separate entrance/handling.
lukeQuote: they went upon the housetop, and let him down through the tiling with his couch into the midst before Jesus.
anabQuote: The houses were underground structures with an aperture like the mouth of a well by which to enter, but they were broad and spacious below.
verification: Dwellings entered from above through the roof aperture, descending into the broad space below — literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: The Armenian houses' human occupants 'descended by a ladder' while the beasts' entrance was dug out - paired with the palsied man lowered bodily through the roof-opening.

title: Journey's end: eating and drinking at 'the Table' of the kingdom
claim: The long march's promised end is reached at Trapezus - Greek trapeza, 'table' - where the wanderers are entertained and given oxen, wheat and wine, and pay their vowed thank-offerings; Jesus promises his fellow travelers that they will 'eat and drink at my table in my kingdom.'
lukeQuote: That ye may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom, and sit on thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel.
anabQuote: The men of Trapezus supplied the army with a market, entertained them, and gave them, as gifts of hospitality, oxen and wheat and wine.
verification: Trapezus/trapeza ('table') at journey's end — name-decode, flagged. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: WORDPLAY FLAGGED: depends on decoding the place-name Trapezus/trapeza ('table'), exactly the name-decode genre Atwill employs.

title: Young colts, kept for the king and never yet ridden, requisitioned by the lord
claim: Young horses/colts being reared - 'tribute for the king,' hence not yet ridden - are taken from villagers by the lord/generals with a justification offered to the owner, and the owner is compensated (an old horse given back / 'the Lord hath need of him'); a colt apiece is assigned for the leaders' use.
lukeQuote: ye shall find a colt tied, whereon yet never man sat: loose him, and bring him hither.
anabQuote: For himself he took his pick of the colts, and gave a colt apiece to each of his fellow-generals and officers.
verification: Colts reared as 'tribute for the king,' requisitioned with the owner dialogue; 'never yet ridden' is inferred, not stated. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Same section carries the owner's dialogue 'For whom are the horses being bred?' 'They are tribute for the king' - the royal-claim formula answering 'Why loose ye the colt?'

title: Soldiers and their wages
claim: Soldiers as a class confronted over pay: John tells soldiers to do no violence and be content with wages; the Ten Thousand pillage for want of pay and are bought off with a promise of regular monthly wages (later cheated).
lukeQuote: And the soldiers likewise demanded of him, saying, And what shall we do? And he said unto them, Do violence to no man, neither accuse any falsely; and be content with your wages.
anabQuote: I can promise you, if you once leave these waters, to furnish you with regular monthly pay, dating from the first of the month
verification: Soldiers pillaging for want of pay, bought off with the promise of regular monthly wages — literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Typological inversion: John's ethic for soldiers reads as a corrective of mercenaries who take provisions by force when unpaid.

title: The temptation to seize power and territory
claim: A leader surveys a vast prospect, is tempted with acquiring territory and power for himself (founding a kingdom/city), keeps the deliberation secret, and finally renounces the ambition.
lukeQuote: All this power will I give thee, and the glory of them: for that is delivered unto me; and to whomsoever I will I give it.
anabQuote: how noble an opportunity to acquire new territory and power for Hellas, by the founding of a colony
verification: The colony-founding temptation surveyed and renounced — interpretive. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Xenophon gazes on the host as the devil shows all kingdoms 'in a moment of time'; he sacrifices privately over it and later renounces: 'I have done with that dream' (5.6.30). Jesus refuses the same offer outright.

title: The healer defense
claim: A leader answers critics of his harsh treatment of the wayward with a medical analogy: the physician/surgeon hurts people for their own good.
lukeQuote: They that are whole need not a physician; but they that are sick.
anabQuote: Does not the surgeon also cauterise and cut us for our good?
verification: The surgeon who cuts and cauterises us for our good, in a self-defense speech against murmurers — same analogy, same setting. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Both occur in self-defense speeches against murmuring accusers; cf. also 'Physician, heal thyself' (Luke 4:23).

title: Asleep on the voyage home
claim: Sailing homeward while stretched out asleep aboard ship: the war-weary soldier's wish to sail 'stretched out in sleep' like Odysseus; Jesus falls asleep as they sail across the lake.
lukeQuote: But as they sailed he fell asleep: and there came down a storm of wind on the lake; and they were filled with water, and were in jeopardy.
anabQuote: since here we have the sea before us, to sail on and on, 'stretched out in sleep,' like Odysseus, and so to find myself in Hellas
verification: Odysseus asleep on the homeward voyage — allusion-level. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Homeric typology: both invoke the figure of the sleeper carried home over the water; in Luke the sleep is interrupted by the storm the sleeper then masters.

title: Swine on the mountain above the ravine
claim: Stray swine on a mountainside beside a tremendously deep ravine with a steep single-file descent, and a rush of a body of more than two thousand across it; Luke has many swine feeding on the mountain that rush down a steep place.
lukeQuote: And there was there an herd of many swine feeding on the mountain: and they besought him that he would suffer them to enter into them.
anabQuote: except here and there a stray pig or bullock or other animal which had escaped the fire there was nothing to capture
verification: Stray swine plus the two-thousand-strong rush — composite across sections. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: The storming party 'amounted to more than two thousand' (5.2.1-5.2.5), matching the two thousand swine of the parallel tradition; Luke's own account keeps the swine, mountain, and steep plunge.

title: The maddened rush into the water and drowning
claim: A crowd seized as if by madness (Xenophon: 'like that to which dogs are liable') rushes headlong, its victims plunge into the water, and those in the water drown/are choked; Luke's demons drive the herd violently into the lake to be choked.
lukeQuote: and the herd ran violently down a steep place into the lake, and were choked.
anabQuote: fled with all speed and threw themselves into the sea, in which proceeding they were imitated by some few of our own men, and all who did not know how to swim were drowned
verification: The madness simile, the headlong flight into the sea, the non-swimmers drowned — literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Same section says the panicked mob acted as if 'some madness had seized us, like that to which dogs are liable' and hunted Zelarchus toward the sea 'as if a wild boar or a stag had been started' - possession-like frenzy ending in mass drowning.

title: The savage man who strips clothes and must be bound
claim: A violent, uncontrollable man associated with stripped clothing who must be restrained with bonds, described in dog/beast terms with a day-night regimen; Luke's demoniac wears no clothes, is bound with chains and fetters, and breaks them.
lukeQuote: he was kept bound with chains and in fetters; and he brake the bands, and was driven of the devil into the wilderness
anabQuote: he has stripped several citizens of Cotyora of the clothes on their backs. If then you are wise, you will treat this personage in a way the contrary to that in which men treat dogs
verification: The violent man strips others of their clothes; the demoniac strips himself — inversion. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Boiscus strips others; the demoniac strips himself - a parodic inversion. Both are managed by binding/loosing, day versus night.

title: Divine provision of loaves and meat for the multitude
claim: A deity personally provides loaves, meat, and festal food to a whole multitude of banqueters at an open feast; the setting features a stream in which fish are found; Luke's Jesus multiplies loaves and fishes for the banqueting multitude.
lukeQuote: Then he took the five loaves and the two fishes, and looking up to heaven, he blessed them, and brake, and gave to the disciples to set before the multitude.
anabQuote: The goddess herself provided for the banqueters meat and loaves and wine and sweetmeats
verification: 'The goddess herself provided for the banqueters meat and loaves,' beside fish-bearing streams — the divine host feeding the multitude. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Same section: 'in both streams fish and mussels are to be found' - loaves plus fish at a sacred meal where the god is the host.

title: Fire from a god upon the hostile village
claim: Travelers attacked by a hostile settlement are delivered when a god sends fire that consumes the village houses; in Luke the disciples ask for exactly this against the village that would not receive them, and Jesus forbids it.
lukeQuote: Lord, wilt thou that we command fire to come down from heaven, and consume them, even as Elias did?
anabQuote: some god gave them a means of safety. All of a sudden, by whatsoever hand ignited, a flame shot up; it came from a house on the right hand
verification: A god's fire consumes the hostile village as deliverance; Luke's disciples request exactly this and are refused — elements literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Typological inversion: Xenophon reads the god-sent flame as a lesson and burns the rest of the village; Jesus rebukes the disciples - 'the Son of man is not come to destroy men's lives, but to save them.'

title: Burying the not-yet-dead
claim: A man excuses himself from carrying/following in order to bury someone who is not in fact dead; the leader rebukes the would-be burier. Xenophon strikes the man digging a grave for a comrade who twitches alive; Jesus: let the dead bury their dead.
lukeQuote: Jesus said unto him, Let the dead bury their dead: but go thou and preach the kingdom of God.
anabQuote: you were digging a trench with intent to bury the man; I pulled up and said something in commendation; as we stood by the poor fellow twitched his leg, and the bystanders all cried out, 'Why, the man's alive!'
verification: The grave dug for a man still alive, with the rebuke — connected to Luke's saying interpretively. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Xenophon caps it with the same paradox: 'we shall all one day be dead, but that is no reason why meantime we should all be buried alive.'

title: Cities judged by market and reception of the sick
claim: Itinerants entering cities where reception is defined by two tests - being given food (a market) and having the sick received/healed; cities failing both tests are denounced. The Cotyorites refuse both a market and shelter for the sick.
lukeQuote: And into whatsoever city ye enter, and they receive you, eat such things as are set before you:
anabQuote: for the latter would neither provide them a market nor receive their sick within their walls
verification: Cities condemned for giving no market and refusing the sick — Luke's two reception tests, literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Luke 10:9 adds 'heal the sick that are therein'; Xenophon's defense speech (5.5.18) turns entirely on cities that gave a market versus those that shut their gates, exactly Luke's receive/receive-not dichotomy.

title: The half-dead man by the road compelled to be carried
claim: A man lies helpless and half-dead on the road; others would pass by or abandon him; one person is made to lift and carry him to save his life, at cost and against convenience.
lukeQuote: A certain man went down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and fell among thieves, which stripped him of his raiment, and wounded him, and departed, leaving him half dead.
anabQuote: A man was left behind from inability to proceed farther; I recognised the poor fellow sufficiently to see that he was one of ours, and I forced you, sir, to carry him to save his life
verification: The man left by the way from inability to proceed; another compelled to carry him to save his life — literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: The mule-driver who wants to leave/bury the man plays the priest-and-Levite role; Xenophon plays the Samaritan by compulsion.

title: The guarded strong man overcome and his spoils divided
claim: A king/strong man kept under guard in his own citadel with his goods; a stronger force comes upon him, overcomes him, and his stronghold is pillaged and its treasures divided.
lukeQuote: But when a stronger than he shall come upon him, and overcome him, he taketh from him all his armour wherein he trusted, and divideth his spoils.
anabQuote: Their king, who sat in his wooden tower or mossyn, built on the citadel (there he sits and there they maintain him, all at the common cost, and guard him narrowly), refused to come forth
verification: The king guarded in his citadel; the stronghold pillaged and its treasures taken — literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: The same section has the Hellenes 'pillaging and ransacking these places' and discovering the treasures - the dividing of the spoils.

title: The blood of the slain messengers required
claim: Blood-guilt for murdered heralds/prophets hangs over the community: the blood of the sent ones is 'upon the hands' / 'required of this generation,' and even burial of the dead becomes impossible.
lukeQuote: That the blood of all the prophets, which was shed from the foundation of the world, may be required of this generation
anabQuote: Who indeed would care to carry a flag of truce, or go as a herald with the blood of heralds upon his hands?
verification: 'The blood of heralds upon his hands' — corporate guilt for slain envoys, formal purification required — literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Both texts make the killing of envoys a corporate pollution: Xenophon has the army formally purified; Luke has the guilt 'required' of the generation. Same section laments that the corpses cannot now be safely buried.

title: The hoarded ancestral stores and the sudden end
claim: Great stores of grain and goods laid up over years ('ancestral stores' / barns for 'many years'); the owners perish suddenly (burnt in their tower / soul required that night); the hoard passes to others.
lukeQuote: But God said unto him, Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee: then whose shall those things be, which thou hast provided?
anabQuote: The Hellenes, pillaging and ransacking these places, discovered in the different houses treasures and magazines of loaves, pile upon pile
verification: Piled ancestral stores passing to others at their owners' sudden end — interpretive. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Luke's 'whose shall those things be, which thou hast provided?' is answered concretely in Xenophon: the invaders eat the dead men's stores.

title: Keeping watch in shifts while awaiting the promised return
claim: A leader departs by sea promising to return; the community left behind is organized to keep watch in successive shifts through the night so as not to be caught off guard.
lukeQuote: And if he shall come in the second watch, or come in the third watch, and find them so, blessed are those servants.
anabQuote: I propose then that we should have regular outposts round the camp. If we take it in succession to do picket and outlook duty, the enemy will be less able to harry us
verification: Watch kept in succession while awaiting a promised return — generic military practice. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Both watch-schemes are instituted precisely for the interval of waiting for one who said he would come back (Cheirisophus / the lord); Cheirisophus, like the delayed lord, does not arrive (5.3.1).

title: Discerning the south wind and the sky-signs
claim: A speaker appeals to the crowd's ability to read the sky - the named south wind versus the other quarter, and the sun's course - as proof they cannot be deceived about the real situation before them.
lukeQuote: And when ye see the south wind blow, ye say, There will be heat; and it cometh to pass.
anabQuote: it is Boreas, the north wind, who bears the mariner out of Pontus towards Hellas, and the south wind inwards towards the Phasis
verification: Named-wind weather-lore as proof the crowd cannot be deceived about what faces them — the same rhetorical move. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Xenophon: 'you know where the sun rises and where he sets... is that a point in which a man might hope to cheat you?' Luke: 'ye can discern the face of the sky... how is it that ye do not discern this time?' Same rhetorical move, same wind-lore.

title: The multitude jostling to enter the gate
claim: A proclamation to enter is followed by a surging multitude fighting its way through the portals, with counter-currents of people pressing in and being forced back - many seeking to enter and not able.
lukeQuote: Strive to enter in at the strait gate: for many, I say unto you, will seek to enter in, and shall not be able.
anabQuote: In poured the surging multitude, and the counter-current of persons elbowing their passage in prevailed over the stream of those who issued forth
verification: The proclamation to enter; the surging multitude jostling at the portals, the counter-current forced back — literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Same section: the herald proclaims 'Enter all who are minded' and 'mighty was the jostling about the portals'; cf. Luke 16:16 'every man presseth into it.'

title: Stoning them that are sent
claim: Envoys sent on a peaceful errand (ambassadors offering burial and reconciliation / prophets sent to the city) are stoned to death by the very people they were sent to.
lukeQuote: which killest the prophets, and stonest them that are sent unto thee
anabQuote: The three men--ambassadors, mark you--were slain, stoned to death
verification: 'Ambassadors, mark you — were slain, stoned to death' — them that are sent, stoned — literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Xenophon even underlines the sent-ness ('ambassadors, mark you'), as Luke does ('them that are sent'). The Colchian heralds and market clerks were likewise stoned (5.7.1).

title: The king with ten thousand takes counsel against a greater force
claim: A war-council weighing whether a force can meet a vastly larger army in the field, concluding it cannot, and opting instead for a peaceful course sealed by sending an embassy. The deliberating army is itself the famous Ten Thousand.
lukeQuote: what king, going to make war against another king, sitteth not down first, and consulteth whether he be able with ten thousand to meet him that cometh against him with twenty thousand?
anabQuote: supposing further, you were able to win an engagement in the plain against not only their cavalry but their more than one hundred and twenty thousand infantry
verification: Ten thousand counting the cost against a hundred and twenty thousand, then sending the embassy — literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Xenophon himself counts the army as 'something like ten thousand with swords in your hands' (5.7.6); after the counsel they vote for the sea route and 'the ambassadors bade them send an embassy, which they did' (5.6.9) - Luke's 'sendeth an ambassage, and desireth conditions of peace.'

title: The fatted ones of the feast
claim: Festal hospitality centered on a deliberately fattened creature displayed/served for celebration: the wealthy exhibit their fatted children fed up for show; the father kills the fatted calf fed up for the feast of the returned son.
lukeQuote: And bring hither the fatted calf, and kill it; and let us eat, and be merry:
anabQuote: these would entertain them with exhibitions of fatted children belonging to the wealthy classes, fed up on boiled chestnuts until they were as white as white can be
verification: 'Fatted' children exhibited for show against the fatted calf — wordplay, flagged. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Wordplay flag: hinges on the shared epithet 'fatted' in a hospitality scene; read typologically as grotesque parody (fatted children of the rich barbarians versus the fatted calf for the returning prodigal).

title: Stoned or drowned in the sea
claim: The same paired fates for offenders/victims: death by stones or death by the sea - those who did not save themselves by leaping into the sea were stoned; better a millstone and the sea than to offend.
lukeQuote: It were better for him that a millstone were hanged about his neck, and he cast into the sea, than that he should offend one of these little ones.
anabQuote: they would repeat the violence with which they had lately treated the heralds of the Colchians and the clerks of the market; when all who did not save themselves by jumping into the sea were stoned to death
verification: Stoned or fled into the sea — the victim/offender roles are inverted. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: In both, the stone-versus-sea alternative attaches to offenses against protected persons (heralds and clerks / the little ones); the millstone is itself a stone that drowns.

title: Of the men together, some taken and one left
claim: A fixed numeric sorting of men grouped together: in each canoe three men, of whom two are taken out into the ranks and the third is left behind; Luke's pairs in one bed or field, one taken and the other left.
lukeQuote: in that night there shall be two men in one bed; the one shall be taken, and the other shall be left.
anabQuote: There were three men in each, two of whom disembarked and fell into rank, whilst the third remained
verification: Three in each canoe, two taken out and the third left — the ratio is inverted. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Read as an inversion of the ratio (two taken, one left versus one taken, one left); the sorting in both cases decides who joins the decisive event and who stays.

title: Wait here till I come
claim: A trusted figure departs by sea to obtain what the community needs (ships / a kingdom), leaving the group behind with the explicit instruction to hold their station until his return, in nearly identical words.
lukeQuote: And he called his ten servants, and delivered them ten pounds, and said unto them, Occupy till I come.
anabQuote: All you have to do, if you are really minded to go home by sea, is to wait here till I come
verification: 'Wait here till I come' from the departing principal, the interval becoming the test — phrase and structure literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Distinctive shared formula 'till I come' from a departing principal; in both stories the interval of waiting becomes the test of the group's conduct (Cheirisophus in fact never returns in Book 5, like the delayed nobleman).

title: Deposits under guard at the Table (Trapezus/trapeza)
claim: Goods/money laid up for safekeeping under appointed guards pending the owner's return, with compensation reckoned - at Trapezus, whose name is the Greek word (trapeza, 'table') that Luke 19:23 uses for 'bank.'
lukeQuote: Wherefore then gavest not thou my money into the bank, that at my coming I might have required mine own with usury?
anabQuote: they took out the freights and appointed guards to keep an eye on their preservation
verification: Freights impounded under guard off Trapezus — name-decode, flagged. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Name-decode flag: KJV 'bank' renders Greek 'trapezan' (table), the root of Trapezus, the city off which the freights are impounded and guarded; the army also agrees on a fare, 'repaying kindnesses in kind' (5.1.10) - the increase due at the master's coming.

title: Requisitioning transport with an answer for the owners
claim: Followers are directed to requisition transport belonging to others for the leader's journey, with a prepared formula answering the owners' objection and a framework of repayment/return.
lukeQuote: And if any man ask you, Why do ye loose him? thus shall ye say unto him, Because the Lord hath need of him.
anabQuote: we have only to ask the loan of some war-ships from the men of Trapezus, and we can bring them into port, and safeguard them with their rudders unshipped
verification: Requisitioned transport justified as a loan answered by need — interpretive. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Both requisitions are framed as loans justified by need and eventual restitution; in the same passage a fare is voted for the impressed crews, 'on the principle of repaying kindnesses in kind.'

title: The trench cast about the doomed city
claim: A city encircled by a trench and rampart, kept in on every side, besieged, and finally destroyed utterly - Luke's prophecy of enemies casting a trench about Jerusalem and laying it even with the ground.
lukeQuote: thine enemies shall cast a trench about thee, and compass thee round, and keep thee in on every side
anabQuote: there was a trench running round it, mounded up some breadth, with a stockade on the top of the earthwork and a close-packed row of wooden bastions
verification: A trench and stockade running round the city, which is then burnt down entirely — literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: The Drilae metropolis is then annihilated: 'the whole city was burnt down, houses, turrets, stockading, and everything belonging to it' (5.2.27) - matching 'shall lay thee even with the ground... not leave in thee one stone upon another.'

title: The interrogation about the blows
claim: A public scene turning on identifying blows - who struck, whom, where, and when: Jesus, beaten and blindfolded, is taunted to prophesy who smote him; Xenophon, accused of beating men, demands the accuser state where and when he was struck.
lukeQuote: And when they had blindfolded him, they struck him on the face, and asked him, saying, Prophesy, who is it that smote thee?
anabQuote: Against Xenophon a charge was brought by certain people, who asserted that they had been beaten by him, and framed the indictment as one of personal outrage with violence
verification: The trial about who struck whom — inversion. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Typological inversion: in Xenophon the striker stands trial and cross-examines the struck man about the blows and is vindicated; in Luke the struck one is mockingly examined about his striker and condemned.

title: The outmatched king sends an embassy desiring conditions of peace
claim: A weaker ruler facing a stronger army does not fight but sends ambassadors bearing gifts to ask terms of peace; the stronger side deliberates in counsel before answering (Luke's king 'sitteth not down first, and consulteth'; the generals 'would consult with the army about the matter').
lukeQuote: Or else, while the other is yet a great way off, he sendeth an ambassage, and desireth conditions of peace.
anabQuote: sent ambassadors to the Hellenes, bearing horses and fine apparel, and charged with a proposal on the part of Corylas to make terms with the Hellenes on the principle of mutual forbearance from injuries
verification: The weaker ruler sends ambassadors bearing gifts to ask terms of peace; the stronger side takes counsel — literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Corylas of Paphlagonia plays the king who cannot meet the stronger force; Luke's parable is read as a type of exactly this embassy scene, and the terms granted are 'mutual abstinence from injuries' - conditions of peace.

title: Struck down, stripped, and left lying as dead
claim: A man is struck by another, falls, is stripped by the one who struck him, who then departs; the victim is left lying as one dead and is carried off by bystanders. Same action sequence as the Good Samaritan opening: struck, stripped, departed, left half dead.
lukeQuote: A certain man went down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and fell among thieves, which stripped him of his raiment, and wounded him, and departed, leaving him half dead
anabQuote: Then he that gave the blow stripped the other of his arms, and marched off chanting the "Sitalcas," whilst others of the Thracians bore off the other, who lay as if dead, though he had not received even a scratch
verification: Struck, stripped by the striker who departs, left lying as dead, borne off by others — the Samaritan opening, literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Typological inversion: the Thracian 'death' is a staged sham ('as if dead... not even a scratch') beside the man left genuinely 'half dead'; in both, third parties carry the fallen man away.

title: The ploughman-sower who keeps looking back loses everything
claim: A man simultaneously ploughs (drives a yoke of oxen) and sows, and while doing so keeps turning about to look behind him; because of what comes on him from behind he is bound and his team driven off. Luke: the man who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is disqualified.
lukeQuote: No man, having put his hand to the plough, and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God.
anabQuote: one man lays aside his arms and proceeds to drive a yoke of oxen, and while he drives he sows, turning him about frequently, as though he were afraid of something
verification: Driving the yoke and sowing while 'turning him about frequently' — and the looker-back is bound and loses his team — literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Composite with Luke 11:21-22: in the same dance 'the robber binds the countryman and drives off the team,' as Luke's stronger man overcomes the armed man, takes his armour and divides his spoils; the scene also stages Luke 8:5's sower.

title: Women cast down the great King
claim: Lowly women are credited with overthrowing the great King and driving him from his place. In Luke the claim is spoken by a woman (the Magnificat); in Xenophon it is the soldiers' boast about their camp women, prompted by a dancing girl.
lukeQuote: He hath put down the mighty from their seats, and exalted them of low degree.
anabQuote: it was the women who routed the great King, and drove him out of camp
verification: 'It was the women who routed the great King' — phrase-level. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Typological: the great King of Persia stands for 'the mighty' put down by those of low degree; both boasts of a humbled monarch are voiced in a context of low-status women exalted.

title: Offered supreme power, he consults God and refuses
claim: A man is offered sole rule over all ('all this power' / the sole generalship of the whole army); he is genuinely tempted ('he had a strong desire to hold the supreme command'), refers the decision to God, and refuses the offered sovereignty on divine authority.
lukeQuote: And the devil said unto him, All this power will I give thee, and the glory of them: for that is delivered unto me; and to whomsoever I will I give it.
anabQuote: the god as plainly as might be gave him a sign, neither to demand the generalship, nor, if chosen, to accept the office
verification: Offered the supreme command, genuinely desiring it, he refers the choice to the god and refuses — literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Xenophon says 'from such sovereignty I must needs hold myself aloof,' as Jesus refuses all the kingdoms to serve God only; in both the refusal follows explicit appeal to heaven against a real inward temptation.

title: The eagle omen of glory and suffering, gathered to its food
claim: An eagle appears as a portent of a coming day of both glory and suffering; the interpretation turns on the eagle and its food/prey ('the eagle seizes his food, not when seated, but on the wing' / 'wheresoever the body is, thither will the eagles be gathered').
lukeQuote: And they answered and said unto him, Where, Lord? And he said unto them, Wheresoever the body is, thither will the eagles be gathered together.
anabQuote: how an eagle screamed on his right hand from the east, and still remained perched, and the soothsayer who was escorting him said that it was a great and royal omen; indicating glory and yet suffering
verification: The royal eagle omen of glory and suffering — symbol-level. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Symbol flag: eagle as royal/imperial omen. In Luke the eagle-and-body saying answers a question about the day of the Son of man; in Xenophon the eagle foretells a career of glory and hardship, expounded through how the eagle takes its food.

title: Rage over the head seat at the dinner of friends
claim: A dinner among friends becomes the scene of a quarrel about who must be given the chief place at the table; the man/nation of rank is said to fly into a rage if not seated at the head - exactly the love of 'the highest room' Luke mocks.
lukeQuote: When thou art bidden of any man to a wedding, sit not down in the highest room; lest a more honourable man than thou be bidden of him
anabQuote: the Lacedeamonians are to fly into a rage because a number of friends have met together to dinner, and omitted to choose a Lacedaemonian to sit at the head of the table
verification: Rage over the head seat at a dinner of friends — the highest-room satire, literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Cf. Luke 22:24-26, the strife at supper over who should be greatest and the Gentile rulers who lord it: Agasias's joke turns the generalship itself into the head seat at a dinner of friends.

title: The deep cleft down to Hades and bringing one up from the dead
claim: A named landmark where the world of the dead is reached through a great depth: Heracles descended there to bring up a denizen of Hades, and the marks of the descent are still shown. Luke's Hades scene turns on the same two ideas - an impassable great deep between the living and the dead, and the request that one be sent up from the dead.
lukeQuote: And beside all this, between us and you there is a great gulf fixed: so that they which would pass from hence to you cannot; neither can they pass to us, that would come from thence.
anabQuote: where Heracles is said to have descended to bring up the dog Cerberus, at a point where they still show the marks of his descent, a deep cleft more than two furlongs down
verification: The Acherusian cleft where Heracles brought one up from the dead — name-decode, flagged. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Name decode flagged: the 'Acherusian Chersonese' carries the name of Acheron, the river of Hades - the geography itself says 'place of the dead.' Inversion: Heracles succeeds in bringing one up from the dead; Abraham denies that any may pass or return from the dead.

title: Bread demanded of friends; the door is shut
claim: A party without provisions (the gifts 'will not afford three days' victuals' / 'lend me three loaves... I have nothing to set before him') importunately demands food of a friendly party; the answer is a shut door - the Heracleots close their gates and man the walls rather than rise and give.
lukeQuote: And he from within shall answer and say, Trouble me not: the door is now shut, and my children are with me in bed; I cannot rise and give thee.
anabQuote: and dismantled the market outside and transferred it within, after which the gates were closed, and arms appeared at the battlements of the walls
verification: The importunate demand for provisions answered by shut gates — composite. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Number echo flagged: 'three days' victuals' beside 'three loaves.' Typological inversion: in Luke importunity finally opens the door; in Xenophon the importunate demand (Lycon 'even went so far as to threaten') shuts the gates for good.

title: We will not have this man to reign over us
claim: Immediately after a man receives sole authority, his subjects band together, repudiate his right to rule over them, and organize against his reign; the Arcadians and Achaeans will not be ruled by an Athenian and a Lacedaemonian, as the citizens will not have the new-made king reign over them.
lukeQuote: But his citizens hated him, and sent a message after him, saying, We will not have this man to reign over us.
anabQuote: It was outrageous that a single Athenian and a Lacedaemonian, who had not contributed a soldier to the expedition, should rule Peloponnesians; scandalous that they themselves should bear the toils whilst others pocketed the spoils
verification: Within a week of receiving sole authority, his subjects repudiate his right to rule them — literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Cheirisophus, like Luke's nobleman, has just received his 'kingdom' (election as general-in-chief) when the revolt strips him: 'the absolute authority vested in Cheirisophus was terminated there and then, within less than a week of his appointment' (6.2.10).

title: The host divided against itself is brought to desolation
claim: A single body divides into factions and the division brings it to the edge of destruction: the army splits into three divisions and the seceding division is promptly routed and besieged, generals slain. The army afterwards decrees death for whoever proposes division again.
lukeQuote: Every kingdom divided against itself is brought to desolation; and a house divided against a house falleth.
anabQuote: In this way the army was now split up into three divisions. First, the Arcadians and Achaeans, over four thousand five hundred men
verification: The host divides into three; the seceding division is promptly routed and besieged; division is then outlawed on pain of death — literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Cf. Luke 12:52, 'five in one house divided, three against two': the one host divides three ways. The sequel decree - 'whoever revived the idea of breaking up the army should be punished by death' (6.4.9) - reads as Luke's maxim enacted as law.

title: Ten commanders, each set over a settlement, and the reckoning of gains
claim: Exactly ten subordinates are commissioned and each is assigned one town/village as his sphere; afterwards there is a rendezvous and reckoning of what each brought back, some with gains and some with nothing ('some with somewhat to show for their pains, others empty-handed' / servants reporting pounds gained, one returning his pound unincreased).
lukeQuote: And he called his ten servants, and delivered them ten pounds, and said unto them, Occupy till I come.
anabQuote: as soon as it was light, each of the ten generals led his company to attack one village, or if the village were large, a couple of companies advanced under their combined generals
verification: Ten commanders, a village apiece, then the reckoning — some with somewhat to show, others empty-handed — literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Number match flagged: ten generals / ten servants; one leader per village mirrors 'have thou authority over ten cities... be thou also over five cities'; the empty-handed captains (6.3.5) mirror the servant whose pound earned nothing.

title: Compassed round about on the hill and kept in on every side
claim: An enemy draws a complete ring around a people encamped on a height, hems them in on every side so that 'they could not stir from their position,' and cuts them off even from their water; reinforcements stream in every minute as the noose tightens.
lukeQuote: For the days shall come upon thee, that thine enemies shall cast a trench about thee, and compass thee round, and keep thee in on every side
anabQuote: with day-dawn they marshalled themselves right round the knoll on which the Hellenes were encamped--both cavalry in large numbers and light-armed troops--while every minute the stream of new-comers grew greater
verification: Ringed right round on the knoll, kept in on every side, cut off even from water — literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Even Luke's 'cast a trench about thee' has its counterpart in the same episode: the survivors save their camp by fencing it 'with a ditch' and a palisade (6.5.1). The siege of the knoll is read as a type of the siege of Jerusalem.

title: Travellers on the road recount all the things that had come to pass
claim: Wayfarers met on the road are questioned about a missing company and recount everything that has happened, including the catastrophe that overtook its leaders; the questioner then acts on the report. In Luke the two on the road tell the inquiring stranger 'the things which are come to pass' about their slain leader.
lukeQuote: Art thou only a stranger in Jerusalem, and hast not known the things which are come to pass there in these days?
anabQuote: came upon some old men pursuing their road somewither, who were brought to him, and in answer to his question, whether they had caught sight of another Hellenic army anywhere, told him all that had already taken place
verification: Travellers met on the road recount 'all that had already taken place' to their questioner — the Emmaus structure, literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Role inversion: in Xenophon the leader questions the travellers; in Luke the travellers unwittingly brief their leader. In both the informants end as guides (Xenophon keeps the old men 'to serve as guides in case of need').

title: Fire sent over the whole land, already kindled before the main body
claim: As the leader advances, fire is deliberately sent across the countryside; the vanguard kindles it ahead so that the main body finds it already kindled and merely completes the work, until the whole country looks ablaze.
lukeQuote: I am come to send fire on the earth; and what will I if it be already kindled?
anabQuote: burning everything combustible they could discover. While the main army, wherever they came upon anything which had accidentally escaped, completed the work, so that the whole country looked as if it were ablaze
verification: The vanguard kindles fire across the land; those who come after find it already kindled and finish the work — literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: The saying is read as the campaign-order it describes: the cavalry 'wherever they set foot, set fire,' and the one who comes after finds the fire 'already kindled' and asks only what remains to do.

title: At daybreak the sought ones are gone; only the left-behind remain
claim: A party sets out at dawn after prayers to find those they seek at the known place and finds no one: the sought company vanished in the night ('at first the marvel was what had happened'), and the mystery is resolved by people remaining at the site who explain the overnight departure. Luke: women at dawn find not the body, are 'much perplexed,' and figures at the tomb explain that he is gone.
lukeQuote: And they entered in, and found not the body of the Lord Jesus.
anabQuote: But no army could they discover, whether of friend or foe; only some starveling old women and men, with a few sheep and oxen which had been left behind
verification: At daybreak, after prayers, the sought company is gone; only the left-behind remain to explain the overnight departure — literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: The dawn sequence is exact: 'at daybreak they offered prayers to the gods... found themselves without knowing it at the very knoll... the Thracians had set off immediately after sundown, and were gone.' The empty knoll plays the empty tomb, the left-behind informants the 'two men' at the sepulchre.

title: The seceders return from ruin and are embraced like brothers
claim: A party that demanded its own way and separated from the body (the Arcadians took their portion - the ships - and set off for themselves), fell into want and near-destruction among strangers, is met again and welcomed with embraces and joy, 'like brothers.'
lukeQuote: But when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him.
anabQuote: both divisions arriving eventually at the same place, were overjoyed to see one another again, and they embraced each other like brothers
verification: The seceded division, rescued from ruin, embraced 'like brothers' with joy — literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Typology: the self-willed division (6.2.10) plays the younger son; the rescue and embrace at Calpe plays the homecoming; the later decree that no one may ever divide the body again plays the restored household.

title: Suspected of founding a city he cannot finish, and mocked for it
claim: A man is publicly suspected of intending to build/found (Xenophon and the would-be city at Calpe); the onlookers react with aversion and derision, and the project is never carried through - the builder who begins and is not able to finish.
lukeQuote: Lest haply, after he hath laid the foundation, and is not able to finish it, all that behold it begin to mock him
anabQuote: their arrival at the place at all seemed very like the crafty design of some persons who were minded to form a city
verification: Suspected of founding a city, publicly derided, and the work never carried through — literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Sequel at 6.4.13: 'Certain people were bold enough to say that Xenophon, out of his desire to colonise the place, had persuaded the seer' - the beholders mock the would-be founder, and the city is never built.

title: The great fever: rebuked in Luke, fatal under the physicians
claim: A principal figure is taken with fever and put under care: Cheirisophus, the army's chosen head, dies 'under medical treatment for fever,' while in Luke the great fever is rebuked and leaves at once. Fever plus medical treatment is the shared concrete pair.
lukeQuote: And he stood over her, and rebuked the fever; and it left her: and immediately she arose and ministered unto them.
anabQuote: Though Cheirisophus, indeed, had already died under medical treatment for fever; and Neon the Asinaean had taken his place
verification: The fever fatal under medical treatment against the fever rebuked — inversion. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Typological inversion, with Luke 8:43 in the background ('had spent all her living upon physicians, neither could be healed of any'): what physicians cannot cure kills the general but is dismissed with a word in the gospel.

title: The crowd gathers thick demanding a sign, and no sign is given
claim: A whole anxious multitude gathers pressing around the act of sign-seeking, and the sign is withheld: the sacrifice is repeated day after day, all invited to witness, and 'the very victims themselves failed,' as the sign-seeking generation is told no sign shall be given it.
lukeQuote: And when the people were gathered thick together, he began to say, This is an evil generation: they seek a sign; and there shall no sign be given it
anabQuote: nearly the whole army, so strong was the general anxiety, flocked round the victims; and now the very victims themselves failed
verification: The whole anxious multitude flocks round the victims and no sign is given; the leader is accused over it — literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: In both scenes the leader is accused over the sign (Xenophon charged with rigging the seer, as Jesus in this same Luke context is charged over Beelzebub); the public is invited to inspect the divination and still receives nothing.

title: Go out now with bags and a weapon
claim: Followers who once travelled unprovisioned are now sent out for supplies carrying both provision-vessels and weapons: 'out came the men with spears, and wine skins and sacks and other vessels' - the kit of 'he that hath a purse, let him take it, and likewise his scrip... sell his garment, and buy one [a sword].'
lukeQuote: Then said he unto them, But now, he that hath a purse, let him take it, and likewise his scrip: and he that hath no sword, let him sell his garment, and buy one.
anabQuote: So out came the men with spears, and wine skins and sacks and other vessels--two thousand strong in all
verification: Out came the men with spears, wine-skins, sacks and vessels — the armed and provisioned sending, literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Typological inversion of Luke 9:3 and 22:35 ('lacked ye any thing?... Nothing'): the armed, sack-carrying expedition ends with five hundred slain by cavalry - the fate the gospel's barehanded missions escaped.

title: Burying the dead before the march can go on
claim: The duty of burying the dead interposes itself on the journey: the column halts again and again to dig graves and bury every body it overtakes on the road before it can proceed. Luke's saying rejects precisely this duty in favour of going on: let the dead bury their dead.
lukeQuote: Jesus said unto him, Let the dead bury their dead: but go thou and preach the kingdom of God.
anabQuote: Before they had gone two miles, they stumbled upon dead bodies, and when they had brought up the rear of the column in a line with the first bodies to be seen, they began digging graves and burying
verification: Halting the march again and again to bury the dead — inversion of the saying; the cenotaph noted. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Typological inversion. The earlier burial detail (6.4.9) buries the five-days dead where they fell and raises 'a great cenotaph' for those not found - a tomb with no bodies, oddly close to Luke's empty sepulchre.

title: The traitor among the companions, mobbed and named
claim: One man out of the fellowship is branded 'the traitor': Dexippus, who 'betrayed his fellow-soldiers' and deserted for gain, intervenes for a promised share of the goods ('Take some for yourself'), hales a companion to the authorities, and the crowd turns on him with stones, calling him traitor - the Judas role: the companion who betrays his own to the authorities for material reward.
lukeQuote: And Judas the brother of James, and Judas Iscariot, which also was the traitor.
anabQuote: the rest of the soldiers present set to work to stone Dexippus, calling him "traitor."
verification: Dexippus, who 'betrayed his fellow-soldiers' for gain and delivers a comrade to the authorities, mobbed as 'traitor' — the Judas role, literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Cf. Luke 22:4-5: Judas communes with the captains and covenants for money; Dexippus is promised a cut of the sheep and delivers a comrade to the Spartan governor. Agasias states the charge outright: 'this same Dexippus betrayed his fellow-soldiers' (6.6.21).

title: A good, honest man given up in exchange for a scamp
claim: Before the foreign governor the choice is framed as one life against another, the innocent against the criminal: Agasias declares that putting him to death means 'sacrificing a good, honest man for the sake of a coward and a scamp' - the Barabbas exchange, where the sedition-and-murder prisoner is released and the faultless man delivered.
lukeQuote: And he released unto them him that for sedition and murder was cast into prison, whom they had desired; but he delivered Jesus to their will.
anabQuote: Be assured that if you put me to death at this time you are sacrificing a good, honest man for the sake of a coward and a scamp
verification: 'Sacrificing a good, honest man for the sake of a coward and a scamp' before the governor — the Barabbas frame, literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Typological inversion: in Xenophon the good man is spared and the scamp discredited; in Luke the exchange runs the other way. Xenophon's own offer - 'I deserve the extreme penalty, and I will submit to undergo it' (6.6.15), though innocent - supplies the voluntary-substitute motif.

title: The governor examines, finds no fault, and presents the prisoners to the crowd
claim: Prisoners stand before the resident governor of the occupying power; the accused protests his innocence ('I neither struck nor shot'); a deputation of the people begs and prays for their release; the governor examines the case, drops the charge ('I have no further charge against the army or any one'), and publicly makes the crowd a present of the men. Luke: Pilate examines, finds no fault, and release of a prisoner to the people is the expected grace of the occasion.
lukeQuote: Ye have brought this man unto me, as one that perverteth the people: and, behold, I, having examined him before you, have found no fault in this man
anabQuote: Here I make you a present of the two men, and I will as you say present myself, and then, if the gods vouchsafe, I will put myself at your head
verification: The governor examines, drops every charge, and makes the crowd a present of the prisoners — literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Typological inversion of the Barabbas scene: the Spartan governor yields to the crowd by releasing the innocent, where Pilate yields by condemning him. Two men are demanded and two given up, as two others stand condemned beside the choice in Luke 23.

title: Soldiers demanding wages, warned against false accusation
claim: Soldiers as a class preoccupied with their wages; Luke's Baptist commands soldiers to be content with wages and accuse no man falsely, which is precisely what Xenophon's unpaid soldiers violate — they grow disaffected and (7.6.10) falsely accuse their general over pay.
lukeQuote: And the soldiers likewise demanded of him, saying, And what shall we do? And he said unto them, Do violence to no man, neither accuse any falsely; and be content with your wages.
anabQuote: As to pay, not a penny was as yet forthcoming, and the soldiers were cruelly disaffected to Xenophon
verification: Unpaid soldiers, cruel disaffection, and the false accusation over pay — the soldier-ethic's elements, literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Typological inversion: Luke's ideal soldier is the photographic negative of the Cyreian soldiery; cf. Luke 10:7 'the labourer is worthy of his hire' as the army's constant refrain.

title: Offer of territory and power for allegiance, refused
claim: A powerful figure offers dominion, fortified places and possessions on condition of personal allegiance ('if you will stay with me' / 'if thou therefore wilt worship me'); the hero refuses the offer and departs free.
lukeQuote: All this power will I give thee, and the glory of them: for that is delivered unto me; and to whomsoever I will I give it.
anabQuote: if you will stay with me, keeping only a thousand heavy infantry, I will deliver to you the fortified places and everything I promised
verification: Fortified places and possessions offered for staying with him; refused — 'only let us go free' — literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Xenophon's refusal at 7.7.51 ('On these terms I may not accept them, only let us go free') plays the role of 'Get thee behind me'; Seuthes also earlier offers Bisanthe 'the fairest of all my possessions' and his daughter (7.2.34).

title: Leader takes to a fisherman's boat as the crowd surges by the lake shore
claim: A pressing, surging multitude at the water's edge; the man in authority gets aboard a fisherman's small boat and puts out from the land. Jesus does it to teach the crowd; Anaxibius does it to flee the crowd of soldiers.
lukeQuote: And he entered into one of the ships, which was Simon’s, and prayed him that he would thrust out a little from the land.
anabQuote: Anaxibius ran down to the sea, and, getting on board a fisherman's smack, sailed round to the acropolis
verification: The crowd surging at the water's edge; the man of authority boards a fisherman's smack and puts out — literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Typological inversion: the admiral who cheated the soldiers escapes the mob on a fisher's boat; the Lord masters the mob from one. Same scene has the panicked Byzantines fleeing 'to the shipping.'

title: A herd of swine destroyed to remove a spiritual affliction
claim: Mass destruction of swine as the mechanism by which a malign supernatural obstacle is expelled and a man is set free: the devils enter the swine which perish; Xenophon offers a holocaust (whole burnt offering) of swine to Zeus Meilichios, the god named as his 'obstacle,' and his fortunes immediately turn.
lukeQuote: Then went the devils out of the man, and entered into the swine: and the herd ran violently down a steep place into the lake, and were choked.
anabQuote: The next day Xenophon went on to Ophrynium and sacrificed, offering a holocaust of swine, after the custom of his family, and the signs which he obtained were favourable.
verification: A holocaust of swine offered to the god named as his obstacle, and his fortunes turn at once — literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Same claim-type as Atwill's Legion/swine parallel; note Book 7 also contains the word 'legions' ('legions of light infantry,' 7.6.24).

title: The would-be leader who cannot feed the multitude
claim: Feeding an assembled multitude as the test of leadership: Coeratadas arrives with bearers of barleymeal, wine and olives, finds he has less than one day's provisions per man, and forfeits his generalship; Jesus, with five loaves, feeds five thousand with twelve baskets over.
lukeQuote: Give ye them to eat. And they said, We have no more but five loaves and two fishes; except we should go and buy meat for all this people.
anabQuote: But when he found that he had a good deal short of a single day's provisions for each man, he picked up his paraphernalia of sacrifice and withdrew.
verification: The would-be leader who cannot feed the assembled multitude withdraws — the leadership-test inversion. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Typological inversion: the failed feast exposes the false shepherd, the miraculous feast vindicates the true one. Coeratadas also fails to get favourable signs at sacrifice, where Jesus 'blessed' the loaves and succeeds.

title: The host breaks the loaves and distributes the fragments to the seated company
claim: A seated multitude; the presiding figure takes loaves, breaks them, and personally distributes the broken pieces — the word 'fragments' appears in both scenes ('taken up of fragments that remained' / 'threw the fragments here to one and there to another').
lukeQuote: Then he took the five loaves and the two fishes, and looking up to heaven, he blessed them, and brake, and gave to the disciples to set before the multitude.
anabQuote: He took up the loaves which lay by his side and broke them into little pieces, and then threw the fragments here to one and there to another as seemed to him good
verification: He took the loaves, broke them into pieces, and distributed the fragments to the seated company — literal, 'fragments' in both. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Also mirrors the Last Supper (Luke 22:19 'took bread... brake it, and gave unto them') and the servant-king saying (Luke 22:27), since Seuthes serves his guests with his own hands, 'leaving for himself the merest taste'; cf. also Xenophon sent to 'collect the scattered fragments' of the army (7.2.3).

title: The reluctant 'exodus' from the city
claim: A departure from the city explicitly named an 'exodus': Luke's transfiguration speaks of the exodos Jesus must accomplish at Jerusalem (KJV 'decease'); Xenophon's soldiers, forced out of Byzantium without provisions, are 'out of heart at their exodus.'
lukeQuote: Who appeared in glory, and spake of his decease which he should accomplish at Jerusalem.
anabQuote: It is the men themselves, who are in want of provisions; that is why they are out of heart at their exodus
verification: Luke's exodos ('decease') beside the soldiers' 'exodus' — a Greek-level decode, flagged. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: WORDPLAY FLAG: rests on the Greek behind KJV 'decease' (exodos, Luke 9:31) matching the translator's English 'exodus' in the Anabasis; not visible on the English surface of the Luke file.

title: The compassionate official who tends the wounded and lodges them, against one who abandons them
claim: A contrasting pair of passers-over and one compassionate figure: Cleander pities the sick and wounded stragglers and insists they be received into houses, while his successor Aristarchus sells four hundred of them; the Samaritan pities the wounded man, binds his wounds, and lodges him at an inn at his own charge.
lukeQuote: And went to him, and bound up his wounds, pouring in oil and wine, and set him on his own beast, and brought him to an inn, and took care of him.
anabQuote: he had made it his business to tend the sick and wounded, pitying them, and insisting on their being received in the houses
verification: He tended the sick and wounded, pitying them, insisting they be received into houses — against the successor who sold them — literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Same three-beat structure as the parable: those charged with care pass by/sell the victims; an unexpected benefactor pities, tends wounds, and pays for lodging.

title: Servants told to prepare and watch; the lord comes at midnight
claim: A lord instructs his men to prepare and wait for his coming at an unspecified hour; he arrives in the night watches (Seuthes 'about midnight'), finds them ready and in order, and blesses/compliments them for it at dawn.
lukeQuote: And if he shall come in the second watch, or come in the third watch, and find them so, blessed are those servants.
anabQuote: Prepare and wait; as soon as the right time comes I will be with you. I shall pick up the peltasts and yourselves, and with the help of the gods, I will lead on.
verification: 'Prepare and wait; I will be with you' — he comes about midnight and compliments the watchers at dawn — literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Same section: 'It was about midnight when Seuthes presented himself with his cavalry,' and at daybreak he compliments the watching troops — 'we find ourselves at dawn of day all happily together, just as we ought to be' (7.3.40).

title: Five at the head of one house, divided among themselves
claim: Exactly five men left at the head of a single body, who immediately split into opposed factions (two for Seuthes, one for the Chersonese, one for Asia): 'the generals could not agree' — Luke: five in one house divided, faction against faction.
lukeQuote: For from henceforth there shall be five in one house divided, three against two, and two against three.
anabQuote: Now these five were left--Neon the Asinaean, Phryniscus the Achaean, Philesius the Achaean, Xanthicles the Achaean, Timasion the Dardanian--at the head of the army
verification: Exactly five left at the head of one body, who immediately divide into factions — literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: The division follows in the same section: 'Now the generals could not agree. Cleanor and Phryniscus wished to march to join Seuthes... Neon's object was to come to the Chersonese... Timasion's one ambition was to cross back again into Asia.'

title: The master shuts the gate; those outside cry to be let in and are disowned
claim: Gates deliberately shut and bolted against a crowd that had just been inside; the excluded stand without, batter and cry for the gates to be opened; the authority's answer is repudiation (Anaxibius proclaims any soldier caught inside will be sold; the master says 'I know you not').
lukeQuote: and ye begin to stand without, and to knock at the door, saying, Lord, Lord, open unto us; and he shall answer and say unto you, I know you not whence ye are
anabQuote: "If you do not of your own accord open the gates," they cried, "we will split them in half"
verification: The gates shut and bolted; the excluded cry for them to be opened and are repudiated — literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Eteonicus 'closed the gates and thrust in the bolt pin'; cf. also 7.6.24, 'Aristarchus shut the gates in your faces each time you offered to approach the town.'

title: The one sent to gather them is repaid with a demand for his stoning
claim: A benefactor sent to gather a scattered people is condemned by the very people he served, who call for his death by stoning; in both, the stoning demand is framed as a settling of accounts ('I should feel I had got my pay in full').
lukeQuote: O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, which killest the prophets, and stonest them that are sent unto thee; how often would I have gathered thy children together
anabQuote: stoned to death as a penalty for all the long dance he has led us, I should feel I had got my pay in full
verification: Sent to collect the scattered; the same crowd later demands his stoning as their 'pay in full' — literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Xenophon was expressly sent 'to collect the scattered fragments' of the army (7.2.3); the same crowd that gave him 'a joyous welcome' later demands his stoning — the Palm-Sunday-to-Passion arc in miniature. Cf. Luke 20:6 'all the people will stone us,' and 7.7.51 'I had better be on the look-out for stones when I return.'

title: The tower undertaking begun without sufficient means to finish
claim: A tower project undertaken and abandoned for insufficiency: Luke's builder lays a foundation and 'is not able to finish'; Xenophon's picked band assaults Asidates' tower, fails to take it, undermines the wall, and must retreat before superior numbers.
lukeQuote: For which of you, intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost, whether he have sufficient to finish it?
anabQuote: So they brought their batteries to bear, but failing to take the tower by assault
verification: The tower assaulted, undermined, and abandoned unfinished — the build/besiege inversion. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Typological inversion (building vs. besieging). Note the paired sequence: Luke 14:28-32 sets the tower saying immediately beside the king-suing-for-peace saying, and Anabasis 7 contains both counterparts (see next entry).

title: Seeing the greater army, the weaker side sends to ask conditions of peace
