claim: The weaker party, perceiving the stronger king's forces arrayed against it, capitulates and sues for terms rather than fight: the Thynians, espying the vast array rank upon rank, come down, supplicate for terms, and profess themselves 'ready to do all that he demanded.'
lukeQuote: Or else, while the other is yet a great way off, he sendeth an ambassage, and desireth conditions of peace.
anabQuote: the Thynians, espying from the mountains the vast array of heavy infantry and light infantry and cavalry, rank upon rank, came down and supplicated him to make terms
verification: Espying the vast array, the weaker side comes down and supplicates for terms — literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: The counting-of-forces motif is explicit in the Anabasis context (Seuthes' force had grown 'treble his former force'). Pairs with the adjacent tower saying (previous entry).

title: Hungry men promised bread 'enough and to spare' in another land
claim: The identical English phrase 'enough and to spare' for food, in the same situation: famished hired men (mercenaries / hired servants) contrasted with a place of plenty they are urged toward — Coeratadas promises the starving army meat and drink enough and to spare on the way to a 'land of plenty.'
lukeQuote: How many hired servants of my father’s have bread enough and to spare, and I perish with hunger!
anabQuote: where they would find themselves in a land of plenty; but until they got there, he would provide them with meat and drink enough and to spare
verification: 'Enough and to spare' — the identical phrase, with hunger, hired men, and a promised land of plenty — literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Distinctive phrase match ('enough and to spare') plus shared context of hunger, hired service, and a promised land of abundance.

title: Thought gone to dwell elsewhere, he returns and they run to meet him rejoicing
claim: A man believed to have departed for good to another's house returns; those watching see him, are glad, and run to meet him; the return is celebrated with livestock (Xenophon comes back bringing six hundred beeves and four thousand sheep; the father kills the fatted calf).
lukeQuote: But when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him.
anabQuote: The soldiers at first maintained that Xenophon had gone to take up his abode with Seuthes, and to receive what he had been promised; so when they saw him they were pleased, and ran to meet him.
verification: Believed gone to another lord's house; when they see him they are pleased and run to meet him — with the livestock — literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Typological framing: the army as the father-house receiving back the one presumed lost to a far lord's table; the cattle Seuthes gives ('of beeves I can give you six hundred head, and of sheep four thousand') furnish the celebration.

title: The unjust steward: entrusted with his lord's goods, accused, keeps the money
claim: A steward figure (Heracleides, who handles all Seuthes' proceeds) publicly accused of wasting/embezzling his lord's goods — he sold the booty and kept the proceeds — and who, fearing to be ousted from his lord's favour, schemes to secure himself.
lukeQuote: There was a certain rich man, which had a steward; and the same was accused unto him that he had wasted his goods.
anabQuote: the man who received the property won by our toil, who took and sold it, and never gave back either to Seuthes or to us the proceeds of the sale, but kept the money to himself
verification: The steward who took and sold his lord's goods and kept the proceeds, afraid of being ousted from favour — literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Cf. 7.5.1: Heracleides 'was afraid of being ousted from the friendship of Seuthes' — precisely Luke 16:3-4, the steward about to be put out who plots how others 'may receive me into their houses.'

title: Make friends with wealth now, so the great man will receive and restore you later
claim: Identical counsel of prudential giving: hand over your money/goods to win a patron's friendship so that, in your day of need, he will receive you — Heracleides tells each dinner guest to give Seuthes presents because he 'will be able to restore you to your native land, or to make you a rich man.'
lukeQuote: Make to yourselves friends of the mammon of unrighteousness; that, when ye fail, they may receive you into everlasting habitations.
anabQuote: now if he should become a great person in these parts, he will be able to restore you to your native land, or to make you a rich man here
verification: Give him your goods now; when he is great he will restore you or make you rich — the mammon counsel, literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: The counsel is spoken by the steward figure (Heracleides) in both frames; Luke puts the moral in the steward parable's coda, Xenophon in the steward's own mouth at Seuthes' supper.

title: The dependent at another's table, figured by the dog at the master's hand
claim: A poor dependent defined by his position at a rich man's table, with dog imagery attached: Lazarus craves the crumbs from the rich man's table and the dogs come to him; Seuthes describes his dependent youth with eyes fixed on another's board 'like a dog watching his master's hand.'
lukeQuote: And desiring to be fed with the crumbs which fell from the rich man’s table: moreover the dogs came and licked his sores.
anabQuote: But I, when I had grown to man's estate, could not endure to live with my eyes fixed on another's board.
verification: The dependent at another's board, the dog at the master's hand — imagery composite. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: IMAGERY/WORDPLAY FLAG: the dog simile completes in the next section ('like a dog watching his master's hand,' 7.2.34). Shared picture: table of another + dog + humiliating dependence, with reversal of fortune following in both stories.

title: The exiled heir returns with hired men to receive his kingdom and slays those who rejected his reign
claim: A nobleman whose house lost its kingdom, raised in a far country at another's court (Seuthes an orphan at Medocus' court), obtains men, returns to 'recover my empire,' and once in power has those who would not submit to his rule slain before him or enslaved.
lukeQuote: But those mine enemies, which would not that I should reign over them, bring hither, and slay them before me.
anabQuote: but the majority of the inhabitants made good their escape, for the hills were close at hand. Those whom he did catch, Seuthes unsparingly shot down.
verification: The exiled heir returns with hired men to recover his empire and shoots down those who resist his reign — literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Backstory at 7.2.28-34: 'my father was driven out of this country... we might easily recover my empire'; the citizens who 'would not' obey are burned out and killed on his return, matching the parable's grim coda.

title: The kingdom-claimant promises graded rewards to his servants by rank
claim: In the same kingdom-recovery story, the claimant promises his followers precisely graded multiples of reward plus authority over land: a cyzicene to the soldier, twice as much to a captain, four times to a general, 'with as much land as ever they liked' — as the nobleman grants ten cities and five cities proportioned to service.
lukeQuote: And he said unto him, Well, thou good servant: because thou hast been faithful in a very little, have thou authority over ten cities.
anabQuote: to the common soldiers a cyzicene, to a captain twice as much, and to a general four times as much, with as much land as ever they liked
verification: Graded multiples for soldier, captain and general, with land besides — the pounds-parable reward table, literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Repeated at 7.6.1 in the same book: 'a daric a month as pay, the officers double pay, and the generals quadruple.' Companion claim to the previous entry — both halves of Luke's pounds parable appear in Seuthes' story.

title: The leader's followers called him 'father' and 'benefactor'
claim: The distinctive title 'benefactor' applied to a leader by his followers, in a discourse contrasting such titles with actual loyalty and true service: Luke — Gentile authorities 'are called benefactors,' but the greatest must serve; Xenophon — 'you called me father... your benefactor,' yet now they seek his death.
lukeQuote: The kings of the Gentiles exercise lordship over them; and they that exercise authority upon them are called benefactors.
anabQuote: in those days you called me 'father!' and you promised you would bear me ever in mind, 'your benefactor.'
verification: 'You called me father... your benefactor' amid the strife over dues — literal, the same honorific. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Both passages occur amid a strife over greatness/dues between a leader and his own men (Luke 22:24 'a strife among them'; the army assembly trying Xenophon). Title-match (euergetes/benefactor) with the same ironic edge.

title: Sell the coat off your back to meet the crisis
claim: Selling one's own garment as the proverbial last resource to raise what is needed: Jesus — sell your garment to buy a sword; Xenophon — the pay should have been raised 'if by no other means, by selling the coat off your own back.'
lukeQuote: and he that hath no sword, let him sell his garment, and buy one
anabQuote: even if you had had to raise a loan to do so, and, if by no other means, by selling the coat off your own back
verification: Raise it 'by selling the coat off your own back' — the sell-your-garment counsel, literal phrase. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Inversion in the same book: the soldiers do the opposite — 'many of the men sold their arms' (7.2.3), selling weapons for want, where Luke's disciples sell garments to arm themselves.

title: Night assault with clubs on his lodging: 'Come out!'
claim: A hostile band comes by night, armed with spears and clubs (staves), against the place where the leader lodges, calling him out by name to his death; both victims protest the treacherous night-time manner of the attack, with fire/darkness imagery ('roast you alive' / 'the power of darkness').
lukeQuote: Be ye come out, as against a thief, with swords and staves?
anabQuote: and they kept calling Xenophon by name: "Come out, Xenophon, and die like a man, or we will roast you alive inside."
verification: By night, with spears and clubs at his lodging, calling him out to die — the swords-and-staves arrest, literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Same section: attackers 'hurling in their spears, others belabouring with their clubs' at the doors by night — Luke's 'staves' (clubs) at the night arrest. Inversion: Xenophon's men leap out with drawn swords and are saved; Jesus forbids the sword and is taken.

title: Seized by an armed band at night and brought to the ruler's stronghold
claim: A night scene at watch-fires: the leader, having gone out by night with a small chosen band, is surrounded and seized by a large armed force (a couple of hundred peltasts) and carried off and brought to the ruler in his guarded stronghold.
lukeQuote: Then took they him, and led him, and brought him into the high priest’s house. And Peter followed afar off.
anabQuote: a couple of hundred peltasts had come up who seized and carried off Xenophon and those with him and brought them to Seuthes
verification: Seized at night by two hundred peltasts and brought to the ruler's stronghold — literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Same scene-furniture as Gethsemane: night, kindled fires, a small trusted party, sudden seizure by a numerous armed band, conveyance to the ruler's well-guarded house/tower. Cf. also 7.2.28-33, swords ordered left outside before entering to the ruler.

title: Revealed by the glare of the night fire
claim: In the same night-seizure episode, fires kindled in the dark cause an approaching/attendant person to stand out and be recognized: Seuthes keeps his watch-fires kindled so that anyone approaching 'would, through the glare of the fire, stand out conspicuously'; Peter, by the kindled fire, is spotted and identified.
lukeQuote: But a certain maid beheld him as he sat by the fire, and earnestly looked upon him, and said, This man was also with him.
anabQuote: whilst any party approaching from the outside, so far from escaping notice, would, through the glare of the fire, stand out conspicuously
verification: Watch-fires kindled so that anyone approaching stands out in the glare — the exposing courtyard fire, literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Companion to the seizure claim — Luke 22:55 'when they had kindled a fire' matches Seuthes' 'watch-fires kindled'; in both, firelight in the courtyard/camp exposes the follower who came after.

title: One offers to die in the condemned man's place; the ruler releases
claim: An execution scene interrupted by substitution: a bystander offers his own life for the one about to be slain ('Would you like to die on his behalf?' — he stretches out his neck to the stroke), the ruler is petitioned, and release follows; Luke's Passion turns on the same exchange-of-lives structure, one released and another delivered up.
lukeQuote: And he released unto them him that for sedition and murder was cast into prison, whom they had desired; but he delivered Jesus to their will.
anabQuote: Seuthes put the question, "Would you like to die on his behalf, Episthenes?" whereat the other stretched out his neck, and said, "Strike, if the boy bids you, and will thank his preserver."
verification: 'Would you like to die on his behalf?' — the neck offered to the stroke, and the ruler releases — literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Typological framing: Episthenes' vicarious offer ('will thank his preserver' — saviour language) prefigures/parodies substitutionary death; inversion in outcome — Seuthes laughs and spares both, Pilate spares the guilty and delivers the innocent.

title: A journey of exactly threescore furlongs ending in dawning recognition
claim: A small party travels precisely sixty furlongs (threescore = sixty) in the evening/night; on the way their perception fails them (the Emmaus pair's eyes are holden; Xenophon's party misreads the deserted watch-fires and thinks Seuthes gone) until the truth dawns — Luke: 'their eyes were opened'; Xenophon: 'the explanation dawned on him.'
lukeQuote: And, behold, two of them went that same day to a village called Emmaus, which was from Jerusalem about threescore furlongs.
anabQuote: in the night they set off to visit the army of Seuthes, sixty furlongs distant
verification: A night journey of exactly sixty furlongs ending in dawning recognition — number and structure literal. Quotes verified verbatim against KJV/Dakyns. Miner note: Exact distance match (60 stadia). Further Emmaus texture in Book 7: Xenophon repeatedly tries to depart for home and is constrained to abide ('they begged him not to go away until he had conducted the army,' 7.7.51; cf. Luke 24:29 'they constrained him, saying, Abide with us').
